title: Emberfall items
descriptions: A ring of twined serpents, subtle in its curve and lordly in its fashion. It has the air of an ancient house-token, made not for display alone but for memory, oath, and inheritance.
Two serpents coil around this ring, their joined curves forming an old household seal. Wear has polished the raised scales smooth.

A ring of grave beauty, simple in line yet touched with a power that does not need display. It brings to mind hidden fences, foresight, and the quiet authority of one whose strength is better felt than boasted.
A spare metal band with a carefully finished edge, dignified without ornament. Its quiet presence suggests a treasure kept close rather than exhibited.

A delicate amulet of subtle work, light enough for secret wearing. Something of twilight wood and far music seems to linger about it, as though it had often hung where leaves, starlight, and song met together.
Fine tracery makes this amulet light enough to hide beneath a collar. Its pattern resembles the branching channels of a tidal garden.
A great pearl, pale and lustrous as starlight on still foam. Even unenchanted it seems the treasure of king or Dwarf-lord, gathered from deep waters and long remembered.
A large pearl with a smooth, pale sheen. Such a specimen would command attention in any harbour treasury.
A green jewel of uncommon life, clear and deep as sunlight through new leaves. It has the look of a gem in which healing and youth have somehow been remembered.
Light passes through the deep green stone like sunlight through fresh leaves. The polished setting leaves most of the jewel exposed.

A carcanet of gold and bright stones, wrought with the ambitious splendour of the great Dwarven smithies. Though rich and weighty in appearance, it lies with an order that suggests master-craft rather than mere display.
Gold links carry an array of bright stones in a precisely balanced necklace. Its jeweller arranged the weight with exceptional care.

A dark ring of severe and secretive make, beautiful in a cold fashion and all the more mistrusted for it. One might think it wrought by a mind that prized mastery, concealment, and hidden allegiance above any open honour.
A severe dark band with an immaculate finish. Its beauty has the deliberate coldness of an official seal used behind closed doors.
A plain ring of fine metal, left without device so that craft, gem, or rune may later give it fuller meaning. It seems made as a worthy foundation for some greater work not yet completed.
An undecorated ring of fine metal, ready for a smith to engrave or enchant. Its sound construction offers a foundation for later work.
A simple amulet of good substance, shaped to receive a more particular virtue. It has the air of a prepared vessel, waiting for gem, graving, or enchantment to declare its true purpose.
A plain amulet shaped to accept a stone, inscription, or enchantment. The unfinished surface awaits a purpose.

A hammer of dreadful size, too great for common war and black in all but name. Even at rest it suggests the breaking of gates, shields, and bones by brute dominion rather than by any honest test of strength.
An enormous black hammer whose mass dwarfs ordinary weapons. Its head looks capable of battering a gate from its hinges.

An immense iron crown, forged more to burden and terrify than to honour. Its dark spikes and crushing weight speak not of lawful kingship, but of a lordship founded on fear and the usurpation of light.
A crushing iron crown bristling with dark spikes. It was built to make authority an oppressive physical presence.
An enchanted glowing jewel, akin to a Silmaril, but much less powerful. You can equip it as a light source with a radius of 1 square. It will shine forever.
A small luminous crystal holds a lesser charge of the energy found in dawnseeds. Equipped as a light, it illuminates a radius of 1 square forever.

[neutral]A robe of plain but serviceable cloth, such as a healer, a house-servant, or some learned man among the Edain might wear in hall or by the fire. It is soft, unarmoured, and easily mended, fit to take dye, stitching, or whatever lesser craft a careful hand may add. ||[noble]A robe of fine weave and ordered fall, light upon the limbs and wrought with a quiet grace that recalls the lore-houses of the Eldar. Even unenchanted it has the air of song kept pure, of memory guarded faithfully, and of a mind not easily shaken by shadow. ||[evil]A robe cut for secretive movement and dark uses, its folds deep enough to conceal the hands and its beauty turned toward uneasy ends. One might think it worn by whisperers, corrupters of counsel, or singers whose art had been bent to discord.

[neutral]A soft cloth robe, unarmoured and easy to mend. ||[noble]Fine weaving gives this robe a clean fall and a light touch against the skin. ||[evil]Deep folds conceal the hands within this dark, secretive robe.

[neutral]Armour of tanned hide, plain and weatherworthy, such as huntsmen, scouts, and hard-travelling folk might wear when iron would burden them too greatly. It is practical gear for rain, thicket, and the long road, asking more of endurance than of splendour. ||[noble]The leather has been cured and cut with patient skill until it lies close without stiffness, after the manner of free hunters and wardens who must pass lightly through wood and over broken stone. It suggests quiet watchfulness, hidden roads, and craft joined to song. ||[evil]This hide has been smoked black and laced for harsh service, after the fashion of prowlers sent abroad from the Enemy's walls. It seems made for crouching pursuit, cruel errands, and the kind of stealth that serves suspicion rather than courage.

[neutral]Tanned hide offers practical protection without the burden of iron. ||[noble]Careful curing leaves this fitted armour supple enough for a scout's long patrol. ||[evil]Smoked black hide and tight lacing suit a patrol sent out to stalk fugitives.

[neutral]Leather armour strengthened with iron studs, heavier than a hunter's jerkin but still meant for marching and common battle. It is the sort of harness a practical soldier would trust: often mended, seldom admired, yet worth its keep in hard service. ||[noble]The studs are set with measured craft and the whole fitted so that firmness does not wholly master freedom of movement. It has the look of gear prepared for wardens and delvers of the Free Peoples, who expected long labour, dark ways, and steadfast hearts. ||[evil]Dark hide and black iron have here been joined in a sterner fashion, as though the armour were meant for a cruel watch rather than a fair field. It recalls gate-guards, hard marches, and captains who prized vigilance, fear, and endurance above all mercy.

[neutral]Iron studs reinforce a leather coat built for marching and rough service. ||[noble]The studs follow a measured pattern that keeps the armour firm without unnecessary stiffness. ||[evil]Black iron and dark hide make a harsh uniform for a prison watch.
A suit of armour made of galvorn: a strange shining black metal so malleable that it is thin and supple, yet strong enough to stop blade and dart.
Shining black dusksteel has been beaten thin and supple. Despite its flexibility, the metal can stop blades and darts.

[neutral]A shirt of linked iron rings reaching to the waist, built for the plain needs of war. It is honest mail, prized by guardsmen and campaigning men not for beauty but for the stubborn shelter it gives where blades come close and blows cannot easily be avoided. ||[noble]Here the rings are small, close-woven, and patiently made, as though forged in a proud Dwarven or Elven smithy where craft was held a matter of honour. It has the air of mail prepared for proven warriors who would stand firm beneath terror and bear themselves unshamed in battle. ||[evil]These links are dark, harsh, and somewhat joyless in their making, as though forged for ash-fields and black companies rather than for any free host. It suggests harsh discipline, smoke-stained ranks, and a will that trusts iron more than courage.

[neutral]Linked iron rings form a waist-length shirt for close fighting. ||[noble]Small, closely riveted rings reveal patient workshop skill. ||[evil]Dark, roughly finished links bear the stains of furnace smoke and military service.

[neutral]A long shirt of linked rings that guards the arms as well as the body, heavier than a corslet and better suited to stern work. It is armour for sieges, hard campaigning, and the stubborn press of battle, such as a seasoned captain, house-guard, or man-at-arms might wear when endurance must answer what swiftness cannot avoid. ||[noble]Bright rings are laid here with a grave and masterly patience, making a hauberk fit for a captain or chosen guard among the Free Peoples. Even before enchantment, it speaks of disciplined strength, renowned smithwork, and the resolve to stand fast against dread. ||[evil]A long war-shirt of blackened mail, heavy with the sense of cruel service. Its fashion recalls the harsher armour of Angband, made for wardens and black guards who were bidden to endure pain, keep their ground, and pity no living thing.

[neutral]A long mail shirt protects the body and arms at greater weight than a corslet. ||[noble]Bright, carefully joined rings make a disciplined captain's harness. ||[evil]Blackened rings form the heavy uniform of a guard expected to endure punishment and hold position.

A corslet of linked rings wrought from mithril, the true silver found in the deep mines of the Dwarves. Lighter than leather yet harder than any common steel, it turns aside blows that would shatter iron. Such armour was prized above all others in the Elder Days.
Tiny lumesilver rings form a corslet lighter than leather and harder than common steel. Its costly metal and close linking offer protection beyond ordinary iron mail.

The stripped bones of an orc, foul even in death. The long teeth and crooked limbs speak of a life spent in malice and hard service beneath darker masters. Little remains now but a brittle mockery of the will that once moved it.
Stripped bones lie in a brittle heap, with long teeth and crooked limbs still recognizable. Nothing remains to identify the creature's last orders.

The bare bones of a mortal Man, laid open by time or violence. They are a stern reminder of how swiftly the Younger Children pass from the world, leaving only silence where hope, fear, and labour once had their dwelling.
Bare human bones have been exposed by age or violence. Their silence offers no explanation of how this traveller died.

The fair frame of an Elf, now stripped of flesh and raiment. Even in ruin it keeps something of the grace of the Firstborn, and its sight is grievous, for the Eldar were not made for such a naked end beneath the Shadow.
A slender skeleton retains the proportions of a once graceful figure. Clothing and possessions have vanished, leaving no account of its life.

[neutral]A round shield of wood and hide, light enough to bear through a long day without much complaint. It is the sort of honest defence a traveller, huntsman, or common soldier might carry, modest in its shelter but easy to trust. ||[noble]This shield is lightly borne yet stoutly framed, with the look of work done in some deep and careful smithy that wasted neither timber nor iron. It speaks of enduring craft, ready balance, and the quiet confidence of a free warrior whose gear is meant to last. ||[evil]A round shield darkened by soot, rawhide, and rough handling, with something of the bully's temper in it. One might imagine it in the grip of snarling soldiery beneath a foul banner, made for blows, noise, and the harsh keeping of lesser folk in fear.

[neutral]A round shield of wood and hide is light enough for a day's travel. ||[noble]A stout rim and balanced grip make careful use of timber and iron. ||[evil]Soot and rough handling stain a shield carried in crowded, brutal fighting.

[neutral]A long shield of wood banded with iron, tapering to a point below. It gives broader cover than a round shield, though at some cost to speed, and so suits a man who expects a hard fight and means to endure it rather than dance around it. ||[noble]Well-balanced despite its length, this shield has the air of something made for disciplined northern companies and for stout hearts that must stand under arrow-flight. It suggests ordered ranks, guarded passes, and the patient strength of folk long at war with the Enemy. ||[evil]A long shield of timber and iron, grimly shaped for the crush of ranks and the driving of lesser fighters forward. It seems fashioned for harsh captains and black standards, caring little for grace so long as the shield-wall holds and the order is obeyed.

[neutral]An iron-banded wooden shield tapers toward the ground, offering broad cover at a cost in speed. ||[noble]Its long frame is balanced for steady ranks under arrow fire. ||[evil]Heavy bindings suit a captain who expects the line to advance through a crush of bodies.

A shield of mithril, true silver mined in the deep places of the earth by the Dwarves. Lighter than a shield of oak yet harder than iron, it gleams with a pale light. The Elven-lords and Dwarven-kings alike coveted such shields in the wars of the Elder Days.
Pale lumesilver makes this shield lighter than oak and harder than iron. Its surface retains a clear sheen beneath the grime.

[neutral]A belt-knife of plain good steel, swift in the hand and easy to keep. Many a traveller, camp-warden, or hard-pressed soldier would carry such a blade for common need no less than for danger, and it serves best where there is no room for a longer weapon. ||[noble]A slim bright knife, wrought for a hand both deft and disciplined. It recalls the close-kept blades of hunters, scouts, and high-born wanderers who moved lightly under the stars and trusted a quick sure stroke rather than any weight of iron. ||[evil]A narrow stabbing knife of dark iron, made to slip in close where a foe is least guarded. Its fashion suggests prowlers, cutthroats, and servants of cruel masters who favour silent work, poisoned hurts, and the hot nearness of blood.

[neutral]A plain steel belt-knife serves for camp chores and fighting in cramped places. ||[noble]A slender, neatly balanced blade rewards a quick and disciplined hand. ||[evil]A narrow dark point is shaped for a sudden thrust at close quarters.

A crude blade of orcish make, its edge notched and its iron dark. The orcs of Morgoth favoured such curved swords, forged in the pits of Angband without art or care. It is a weapon of cowardly heart, yet better than none.
A crude curved blade carries notches along its dark iron edge. It is rough issue from a crowded military forge.

[neutral]A short sword of serviceable make, light enough for long wear at the hip and quick enough for the close hazards of road or watch. It is a plain soldier's side-weapon, valued for readiness, sound point, and the ease with which it may be drawn in cramped places. ||[noble]A short sword of clean line and lively balance, such as might be borne by wardens of hidden borders, greenwood hunters, or chosen guards in halls where old craft and stern vigilance were both held dear. It promises speed without meanness and subtle skill without deceit. ||[evil]A squat dark war-blade, fit for tunnel patrols, bullying sentries, and the sudden work of a cruel press. Its make recalls black companies that value quick blood, harsh command, and underhand advantage above any open trial of skill.

[neutral]A short steel sword is easy to draw where a longer blade would catch. ||[noble]Clean lines and lively balance suit a scout or household guard. ||[evil]A squat dark blade is built for tunnel patrols and abrupt close fighting.

[neutral]A sword of good length and balance, the workhorse of the warrior. Many of the heroes of the Elder Days wielded blades of this sort. ||[noble]A long sword of measured balance and honest reach, the kind of blade on which a free warrior might stake both his life and his name. It has the look of a weapon made to answer skill, courage, and open combat beneath the sun or stars.
[neutral]A sword of useful reach and balance, suitable for the daily work of a soldier. ||[noble]Careful shaping gives the long blade a measured, responsive movement.

[neutral]A hand-and-a-half sword, long enough to strike with weight yet not so great that it cannot still be borne beside a shield. It is a practical war-weapon for seasoned fighters who must answer changing need, and who choose usefulness before display. ||[noble]A long sword of lordly reach, made for a warrior trained to rule both measure and moment: shield in the first onset, both hands when the stroke must be finished cleanly. It has the air of the high captaincies of the Eldar and the Edain, where mastery was joined to discipline. ||[evil]A heavy hand-and-a-half blade of grim fashion, better suited to wrathful enforcers than to free champions. One sees in it the temper of furnace-smithies and cruel hosts: jagged strength, domineering reach, and a will to break spirit as much as flesh.

[neutral]A hand-and-a-half sword can accompany a shield or take both hands for a heavier stroke. ||[noble]Its long reach and controlled balance suit a fighter trained to change grips as battle demands. ||[evil]A heavy blade emphasizes an enforcer's reach and force.

[neutral]A great two-handed sword, grave and difficult, taken up only by one with strength enough to govern its full course. It is no common sidearm, but a field-weapon for hard battle, when reach, weight, and a fearless heart must all be trusted together. ||[noble]A great sword of high discipline, terrible in measure yet clean in purpose. It brings to mind the champion-blades of the Elder Kings and captains of the Free Peoples, borne in dreadful hours against troll, dragon, or deathless foe when lesser weapons would not serve. ||[evil]An immense black war-sword, forged for captains who would master a field by terror as much as by slaughter. Its fashion suggests the dark furnaces of the North: fire-hardened, hungry, and pitiless, delighting alike in the breaking of ranks and the spilling of life.

[neutral]A great two-handed sword demands strength and room to govern its stroke. ||[noble]A disciplined smith has balanced the long blade for a champion facing formidable enemies. ||[evil]An immense black blade was made to break ranks through weight and menace.

A blade forged of mithril by the smiths of the Hidden Kingdoms, whose craft in the Elder Days surpassed all others in Middle-earth. It is slender and swift, bright as starlight on still water, and its edge holds keen and true where lesser steel would dull.
A slender lumesilver sword has a bright surface and a durable keen edge. Fine shaping keeps it swift in the hand.

A greatsword forged of star-iron, metal fallen from the heavens in ages past. Harder and keener than any ore of the earth, it was wrought by Elven-smiths into a weapon of terrible sharpness. Its edge can bite through armour that turns aside common steel.
Meteor metal forms a greatsword harder and keener than ordinary steel. Its edge can penetrate armour that would stop a common blade.

[neutral]A plain spear of seasoned wood tipped with iron. Herdsmen, levy-men, and door-guards alike have trusted such weapons, for it is cheap to make, easy to carry, and deadly enough in steady hands. ||[noble]A straight war-spear of clean shaft and bright head, such as the wardens of fair realms might bear upon green marches or white walls. It speaks of long discipline, clear purpose, and watch kept against the fell servants of the North. ||[evil]A black-shafted spear with a narrow killing head, fit for the hands of overseers and cruel watchmen. It seems made less for open valour than for keeping others in fear and for striking Men and Elves from behind a harsher master's line.

[neutral]A seasoned wooden shaft carries a simple iron spearhead. ||[noble]Straight grain and a clean bright point make a dependable guard's weapon. ||[evil]A narrow head tops a black shaft made for an overseer's reach.

[neutral]A great spear of unusual length, meant for both hands and enough room to wield it. It is a grave practical weapon for gateways, stairheads, or open ground, where a man would rather meet danger well before it comes to sword-stroke. ||[noble]A tall bright war-spear, such as gate-guards, wall-companies, and chosen champions might bear in the northern wars. It has the severe beauty of a weapon made to hold the line against fell things before they come within arm's reach. ||[evil]A dark overlong spear whose reach feels less soldierly than predatory. It suggests some fell watcher who would keep living flesh at a distance and draw strength from each deep wound, as though the weapon grudged every drop of blood it spilled to the earth.

[neutral]An unusually long spear needs both hands and space to wield. ||[noble]Its height and bright point suit a defender holding a gate or stairhead. ||[evil]A dark overlong shaft keeps the wielder far from the wounds it inflicts.

[neutral]A long-hafted blade that joins the reach of a spear to the shearing edge of a sword. It is useful in broken ground and crowded battle alike, where a fighter must keep space and still cut hard when the press comes near. ||[noble]A glaive of well-governed curve, such as household guards or picked warriors of high houses might wield. In it are measure, training, and a stern grace, fit for keeping gate, prince, or line with broad strokes laid wide and true. ||[evil]A dark reaping poleblade, apt for jagged work, poisoned edge, and the cruel herding of weaker folk. It looks like the weapon of a captain who drives others before him and cuts down the wavering more gladly than he meets a bold foe face to face.

[neutral]A sword-like blade on a long haft combines cutting power with reach. ||[noble]A controlled curve suits broad, practiced strokes from a household guard. ||[evil]A dark poleblade is built for sweeping cuts through a crowded line.

[neutral]A light axe small enough for the belt and quick enough for the throw. Such a tool serves in camp and on the road no less than in a skirmish, ready for brushwood, kindling, or a sudden hard cast at need. ||[noble]A compact war-axe of Dwarven temper, neatly hafted and close balanced. It has the look of a side-arm borne by the craftsmen-warriors of Belegost and Nogrod, made to bite true against dragon, dead thing, and the crawling horrors of the deep. ||[evil]A dark little axe with a thick wedge-bit, fit for raiders and black-smith work. Venom, soot, and cruel over-weighting seem proper to its kind, and one imagines it cast first from cover or used low and fast in a butcher's press.

[neutral]A small axe serves camp work and can be thrown at need. ||[noble]Neat hafting and close balance make a compact, dependable sidearm. ||[evil]A thick wedge-bit gives this dark little axe a brutal appearance.

[neutral]A broad axe made openly for war. It asks stout arms and good footing, but no subtle craft of the hand; once its stroke is loosed, few harnesses will wholly turn it. It is straightforward gear for a fighter who means to end the matter plainly. ||[noble]A battle axe, soundly hafted and broad of bit, after the grave manner of the Dwarves and the war-folk of Hador. It suggests chosen companions who stood firm against troll, drake, and darker things, valuing a sure stroke more than fury. ||[evil]A black war-axe, iron-bound at haft and neck, fit for the front of cruel companies. Fire, jagged edge, and the bully's delight in breaking Men and Elves seem proper to its fashion; it is a weapon for overseers and hard masters, not for free warriors.

[neutral]A broad war axe demands stout arms and sound footing for its heavy stroke. ||[noble]Careful hafting gives the broad bit a reliable line through the swing. ||[evil]Iron bindings reinforce a black axe made for the front of a harsh company.

[neutral]A huge two-handed axe, costly in strength and space, taken up only when lighter strokes will not serve. It is a grim tool of breach and close war, more feared for its certainty than for any grace in the handling. ||[noble]A great axe of patient and mighty craft, such as a Dwarf-lord or a chosen champion of the Edain might raise in the blackest hour. It carries the memory of deep forges and oath-kept halls, and was made to stand against dragon, dead thing, and terror without yielding. ||[evil]A vast black axe, all menace in head and haft, as though it were forged for executioners and gate-breakers beneath the northern dark. In it lie the cruel fashions of Udun: fire, hooked edge, and a hunger that would draw strength from the wound it makes.

[neutral]A huge two-handed axe demands strength and space for its fall. ||[noble]Patient forging has made a formidable tool for a champion or breach guard. ||[evil]A vast black head and reinforced haft resemble an executioner's equipment.

[neutral]A staff of seasoned wood, shod for hard use at either end. Such staves serve traveller and watchman no less than teacher or healer: a help upon long roads, a measure in dark places, and, if need be, a plain weapon of reach and patience. ||[noble]A well-chosen staff of elder make, such as a loremaster or far-wandering exile might bear. It speaks at once of Tirion's ordered speech, of songs remembered beside Mithrim, and of a strength that endures cold, hunger, and the long labour of the road.
[neutral]A seasoned wooden staff is shod at both ends for road and battle. ||[noble]Straight grain and careful fittings suit a travelling teacher who may also need to defend the road.

[neutral]A hammer made for war rather than the forge, with a compact head meant to dent mail, numb the shield-arm, and break what the blade might only score. It is plain hard-going gear, kin to labouring tools though intended for a harsher craft. ||[noble]A war-hammer of stern Dwarven make, measured in haft and weight with the same care given to an anvil-tool. It recalls the houses of Belegost and Nogrod, and the grim fidelity of those who took hammer in hand against dragon, wraith, and the restless dead. ||[evil]A black-forged hammer with a swollen head and a joyless balance, built to crush through harness by brute certainty alone. One thinks of the furnaces beneath Thangorodrim, where the arts of the smith were bent away from making toward mere domination.

[neutral]A compact war hammer dents armour and jars the shield-arm with a blunt stroke. ||[noble]Measured weight and sound hafting show the precision of a skilled toolmaker. ||[evil]An enlarged black head gives this hammer a harsh, crushing balance.

A broad iron spade for earth, ash, and fallen stone. It is a workman's tool before all else, carried where trenches must be cut or choked passages cleared in haste. In desperate hands it may serve as a clumsy weapon, but its true office is to win a way through rubble. It can be equipped as a weapon and allows you to dig through rubble.
A broad iron spade shifts soil, ash, and fallen stone. Equip it as a weapon to dig through rubble.

[neutral]A heavy mattock, half tool and half weapon, built to bite stone, root, and stubborn earth. Delvers and sappers prize such an implement, for it breaks what the shovel can only shift and may, in a pinch, answer a foe with the same hard stroke it gives to rock. ||[noble]A mattock of grave Dwarven fashion, as though made for the old delvers of Belegost or the long-bearded miners of the North. Even before enchantment it speaks of deep halls, red forge-light, and a people who could turn a miner's tool to war without any shame in the doing. It can be equipped as a weapon and (usually) allows you to dig through rubble, damaged walls or quartz.
A heavy mattock breaks roots, stone, and packed earth, and can serve as a weapon. Equipped as a weapon, it usually permits digging through rubble, damaged walls, or quartz.

[neutral]A plain iron helm, forged to guard brow and temple from the common hazards of war. Such pieces are bought or issued wherever men expect stones, arrows, and the rough nearness of battle; they speak of service, not station. ||[noble]A well-made helm of balanced iron, leaving room for sight, breath, and clear command. It has the bearing of gear prepared for wardens and captains of the Free Peoples, whose armour was meant to steady the hearts of friends no less than to turn the enemy's stroke. ||[evil]A hard-browed war-helm, dark in finish and severe in line. One can imagine it on an orc-sergeant or pit-overseer, where the lowered rim, black visor, or cruel crest served as much to cow lesser thralls as to ward the head.

[neutral]A plain iron helm guards brow and temple against common battlefield hazards. ||[noble]Balanced shaping leaves useful room for sight and breathing. ||[evil]A lowered brow and severe dark finish give a patrol officer a threatening silhouette.

[neutral]A heavy helm enclosing brow, cheek, and face against the first violence of battle. Such gear belongs to the breach, the shield-wall, and the narrow gate, where a warrior must trust iron more than ease and stand his ground beneath a rain of blows. ||[noble]A great helm cunningly shaped so that strength need not wholly smother sight or breath. It has the air of armour made for a lordly champion or gate-captain, one who must meet the onset in person and be known there by constancy rather than by terror. ||[evil]A looming helm that closes the face into something almost less than human. Its fashion suits the rank-drivers of Angband: black captains who led the throng by menace, hid their own weakness behind iron, and wished to be feared before ever they were obeyed.

[neutral]A heavy helm encloses the brow, cheeks, and face for close fighting. ||[noble]Careful shaping preserves sight and breath within a strong enclosing shell. ||[evil]A looming dark faceplate conceals the wearer behind an impersonal mask.

A full-faced helm wrought in a fearsome visage by the smiths of the Dwarves. The Dwarves fought ever in the forefront of battle against Morgoth's hosts, and their smiths devised such masks to strike fear into all who faced them. Its visor withstands the flames of the Enemy.
An enclosed metal helm is worked into a frightening face. Its visor resists flame, a practical feature for troops who must confront fire at close range.

A helm of mithril, true silver from the deep mines of the Dwarves. Lighter than iron yet stronger, it gleams with a pale light that no shadow can dim. The cold and fire of Morgoth's realm alike hold little power against it.
Pale lumesilver makes this helm lighter and stronger than iron. Its metal resists the extremes of both fire and cold.

A crown of worked metal, made as a sign of rule and remembrance rather than for battle. Even plain of gem and device, it lends the brow a certain gravity, as though authority and song might both have worn such a thing.
Worked metal forms a crown meant to mark office rather than serve in battle. Its plain outline leaves room for later ornament.

[neutral]A cloak of serviceable wool, such as a traveller, watchman, or hunter among the Edain might wear against drizzle, ash, and the chill before dawn. It promises no splendour, only shelter, plain concealment, and a little comfort upon the road. ||[noble]A fair cloak of close-woven wool, light upon the shoulders and finished with a care for colour and border beyond mere need. It suggests a gift from some noble house, fit for a trusted messenger or warden who goes abroad bearing memory of brighter halls.
[neutral]Serviceable wool shields a traveller from drizzle and the chill before dawn. ||[noble]Close weaving and a carefully finished border make a worthy gift for a trusted messenger.

A cloak woven of the deepest darkness, its fabric seeming to drink the light around it. It wraps the wearer in shadow, and in the lightless halls of Angband, one who dons it passes unseen as though the night itself were their ally.
The dark fabric seems to absorb surrounding light. Wrapped around the shoulders, it deepens the shadows that conceal its wearer.

The hide of a monstrous wolf, cured whole and made into a dreadful mantle. Its shape invites disguise, and there lingers in it the savage authority of a hunter that was itself long feared in the dark.
A monstrous wolf's whole hide has been cured into a mantle. Its shape offers a disturbing disguise and still suggests the authority of a feared predator.

A dark winged fell, thin and leathern, contrived to hang about the body like the folded shape of some great bat. It seems made for gliding shadow, uncanny disguise, and errands best done beneath a blind moon.
Thin leathery wings fold around this dark mantle. Worn close, they suggest a great bat at rest and invite an uncanny disguise.

[neutral]A shortbow of seasoned wood, quick in the hand and easy to carry through brush or broken ground. It is a useful weapon for hunting, watch-duty, and the sudden skirmish, prized more for ready shooting than for the great force of a heavier bow. ||[noble]A shortbow of choice wood, neatly tillered and well matched to a quick sure hand. One might think of marchwardens under the trees, mariners who keep sharp watch by the grey sea, or hunters of hidden halls, for it speaks of keen sight, light step, and disciplined craft. ||[evil]A shortbow of dark make, horn-bound or harshly backed, such as might be carried by the prowling servants of Angband. It favours sudden shots from covert, harsh pursuit, and the miserable work of scouts who hunt for a host rather than for their own meat.

[neutral]A compact wooden bow is convenient in brush and broken ground. ||[noble]Choice timber and careful tillering suit a quick, accurate archer. ||[evil]Dark backing reinforces a scout's bow made for sudden shots from cover.

[neutral]A longbow of strong stave and patient draw, fit for hunting over open ground or for war where a man has time and space to set his feet. It asks more of the arm than a shortbow, but sends a shaft with greater force and over a longer reach. ||[noble]A longbow of fine grain and careful tiller, made for archers who trust clear sight, ordered ranks, and the far shot taken at the right moment. It calls to mind the sea-watch of the western havens, the guarded woods of the Eldar, and the long vigilant peace before open war returned. ||[evil]A dark longbow of stern and joyless make, blackened or over-hard, as though fashioned for the bitter airs of the North. It has the look of a bow kept by wolf-wardens and black scouts for pitiless ranging and distant slaughter, where the archer need not hear the cry of what he strikes.

[neutral]A long stave demands more strength and space than a shortbow, rewarding the draw with greater force and reach. ||[noble]Fine grain and patient tillering suit distant, deliberate shooting. ||[evil]A dark, stiff stave belongs to a sentry content to kill from far away.

A bow fashioned from the horn of one of the great wyrms that served Morgoth in the Elder Days. The horn is harder than any wood and springs with a terrible strength, sending its arrows with the force and fury of the beast from which it was taken.
A great beast's horn gives this bow exceptional hardness and spring. It demands a powerful draw and sends arrows with formidable force.

[neutral]A simple arrow of ash or birch, iron-headed and feathered for useful service. Such shafts are carried in great number by hunters and soldiers alike, for they are made to be spent, lost, and replaced without much ceremony. ||[noble]A straight and well-matched arrow, balanced with the care of master bowyers. It suggests the guarded arts of hidden realms, where shafts were made not for wasteful shooting but to answer wolf, spider, orc, and darker things that trespassed upon fair lands. ||[evil]A dark-feathered arrow, cruelly headed and fit to carry venom or leave a tearing wound. It seems shaped for fell hunting, when quarry is hounded through fear and pain and the shot is prized as much for mischief after striking as for the strike itself.

[neutral]An iron-headed shaft is feathered for ordinary hunting and military use. ||[noble]Straight grain, matched feathers, and careful balance show a master fletcher's work. ||[evil]Dark feathers and a cruel head give the shaft a menacing finish.

[neutral]Sturdy leather boots for the road, fit for rain, mud, and the daily wear of long going. They are the sort a traveller, hunter, or common scout might prize for dry feet and sound footing rather than for any proud token of house or rank. ||[noble]Good boots, light in the tread and patiently cut, after the woodland fashion of Brethil. They seem made for free folk who move by their own will through thicket, stream, and leaf-fall, keeping long watch without noise or needless weariness. ||[evil]Heavy dark boots, thick at sole and harsh at heel, as though meant for black roads where mercy is not expected. They bring to mind gaolers, march-drivers, and prowling servants of the Enemy, men who pursue by night, kick open doors, and thrive on treacherous ground.

[neutral]Stout leather boots serve long roads, rain, and mud. ||[noble]Light, well-cut leather suits quiet patrols across woodland streams. ||[evil]Thick soles and harsh heels suit prison corridors and forced marches.

[neutral]Greaves of leather and iron, made to spare the shins from stones, low cuts, and the weary battering of a campaign. They are ordinary soldier's armour, valued by those who march far and do not wish every mile to leave its mark. ||[noble]Well-fitted greaves, strapped with the thoroughness of Dwarven smithies and the plain pride of good houses. They suggest hill-folk and mountain-warriors who prized firm footing, ordered march, and the strength to come to battle unwearied. ||[evil]Harsh greaves of iron and hide, built less for speed than for the stamping pace of enforcers. They seem the gear of black-marching troops and road-wardens who drive others before them, caring only that the step remain hard, relentless, and feared.

[neutral]Leather and iron guard the shins against low blows and rough ground. ||[noble]Well-fitted plates and firm straps support an orderly march. ||[evil]Heavy plates favour an enforcer's relentless stamping pace.

[neutral]Greaves of mithril, wonderfully light upon the leg yet harder than iron. Their shape is plain enough that they might serve any seasoned warrior fortunate enough to own so rare a metal, favouring long marches, sure footing, and enduring guard. ||[noble]Mithril greaves of bright and sparing craft, in which Dwarven mastery is turned toward swiftness rather than burden. They seem fit for a chosen marcher or moonlit watch-captain, one who must go far, avoid misstep, and still stand radiant in the last defence. ||[evil]Even this high metal may be bent to darker service: these greaves are severe, close-fitted, and joyless in their economy. They recall the war-gear a black captain would covet, for they promise a tireless march, a louder tread, and endurance without honour.

[neutral]Light lumesilver plates protect the legs without the burden of iron. ||[noble]Precise shaping gives a long-distance marcher protection with little excess weight. ||[evil]Close-fitted pale plates make costly equipment for a relentless patrol captain.

[neutral]Light leather gloves, made to keep the hands from cold, damp, and chafing work. They are ordinary useful things for riding, drawing a bow, handling rope, or labouring in rough weather, with no greater pride than good service. ||[noble]Soft gloves of careful make, preserving warmth without dulling the fingers. They would suit a forester of Brethil or a healer's attendant in a quiet house, where a hand must remain both gentle and ready, whether for herb, bowstring, or the subtle work of aid. ||[evil]Dark gloves, close-stitched and narrow at the wrist, contrived to conceal the hand rather than honour it. They look fit for whispering agents and oath-breakers, whose craft lies in hidden signs, sudden knives, and the small betrayals that open the way to worse.

[neutral]Light leather protects the hands from damp, chill, and chafing. ||[noble]Soft, carefully sewn fingers preserve a delicate touch. ||[evil]Dark, close stitching conceals the hands of a secretive agent.

[neutral]Gauntlets of iron-banded leather, guarding hand and forearm in the rough closeness of battle. They are plain fighting gear, meant for shield-grip, weapon-work, and any hard labour in which a bare hand would soon be bruised or broken. ||[noble]Strong gauntlets with supple joints and a disciplined make, contrived for warriors who must hold fast without losing skill of hand. They suggest stern frontier houses and Dwarven-trained companies that prized steadfast grip, measured force, and service to comrades. ||[evil]Heavy gauntlets with a cruel purpose in every plate and hinge. They seem made not only for war, but for clawing holds, wrenching prisoners, and the deliberate infliction of pain. A gaoler, traitor, or torturer might wear them as gladly as any fighting man.

[neutral]Iron-banded leather guards the hands during fighting and hard work. ||[noble]Supple joints preserve a steady weapon grip within strong plates. ||[evil]Heavy plates and harsh joints suggest equipment for a cruel prison guard.

[neutral]Gauntlets of mithril, light enough that the hand remains quick within them, yet strong enough to turn aside blows that would maim lesser metal. They have the look of costly war-gear for a seasoned fighter who wants both firm grip and freedom of wrist, whether for swordplay or some feat of strength. ||[noble]These gauntlets are wrought with a rarer gentleness, preserving not only strength of hand but delicacy of touch. One might think them fit for a high warrior who must heal as well as strike, or for the trusted servants of a noble house, whose hands were meant to guard life, not merely to take it.
[neutral]Lumesilver plates protect the hands while leaving the wrists quick and free. ||[noble]Fine articulation preserves the delicate touch needed for work as well as battle.

A length of common wood wrapped in pitch-soaked cloth, giving a smoky and uncertain flame. Such torches are cheap, easily spent, and little loved, yet in black tunnels and roofless pits even so poor a light may hold dread a little farther off. You can equip it as a light source with a radius of 1 square. It can hold up to 3,000 turns of light, but begins to sputter when only 100 turns remain.
Pitch-soaked cloth wraps a length of common wood. Equipped as a light, it illuminates a radius of 1 square, holds at most 3,000 turns of light, and begins sputtering at 100 turns remaining.

[neutral]A lantern of brass and glass, made to shelter its flame from draught and dripping dark. Such lamps are prized by scouts, miners, and all who must work below the sun, for their steadier light serves both patient searching and the long watch. ||[evil]A shuttered lantern of harsh brass, the sort one might imagine in the hands of pit-wardens and black patrols. Its light seems less a comfort than an instrument of suspicion, made to search cracks, bars, and faces, and to keep lesser folk uneasy in the dark. You can equip it as a light source with a radius of 2 squares. While you carry brass lanterns and oil flasks, their oil is pooled together. Oil containers use four supply slots: a brass lantern uses two slots and holds up to 5,000 turns, while a flask uses one slot and holds up to 2,500 turns.

Brass and glass shelter a steady flame that, when equipped, illuminates a radius of 2 squares. Carried brass lanterns and oil flasks share their oil across four supply slots: each lantern occupies two slots and holds up to 5,000 turns of light, while each flask occupies one and holds up to 2,500 turns.

A lamp wrought in the manner of Fëanor, the most gifted of all the smiths of the Noldor. It is set with lesser jewels that hold a captured radiance, and shines with a light that no wind may quench. You can equip it as a light source with a radius of 4 squares. It will shine forever.
A crystal lamp encloses a permanent store of radiance that wind cannot quench. Equipped as a light, it illuminates a radius of 4 squares forever.

One of the three great jewels wrought by Fëanor in the Blessed Realm, in which he captured the mingled light of the Two Trees of Valinor before their darkening. Morgoth stole the Silmarils and set them in his Iron Crown, and for their recovery the Noldor waged their long and ruinous war. Their radiance is holy, and no mortal hand may hold them without pain unless their cause be just. Its holy light can break the Oath of Fëanor that binds cursed items. You can equip it as a light source with a radius of 7 squares. It will shine forever.

A dawnseed is a surviving power cell from the failed weather engine, now mounted in the regent's crown. Its cleansing radiance can break the Furnace Covenant on cursed items; equipped as a light, it illuminates a radius of 7 squares forever.
An amulet wrought with an ancient blessing, said to turn aside even death itself at the very last hour. Such grace was rare in the Elder Days, when doom fell swiftly upon the proud.
A life-preserving charm offers its final protection when death is close. Such amulets are prized by crews sent where rescue cannot follow.

[neutral]An amulet of stout and serviceable make, prized by those who would keep their strength through hunger, cold, and the long labour of the road. It has the look of a thing made for endurance rather than display, and speaks of a body meant to outlast weariness. ||[noble]An amulet wrought with a graver and fairer strength, as though some older virtue had been bound within it. Its endurance feels less like stubborn flesh alone than like the patience of deep roots and living stone, kept against wasting by a cleaner power.
[neutral]A sturdy amulet supports the body's endurance through hunger, cold, and labour. ||[noble]Precise workmanship strengthens its quiet protection against physical exhaustion.

[neutral]An amulet of refined craft, worn by those who would keep the spirit clear and the inward senses untroubled. It lends a certain poise to thought and bearing, as though the heart had been taught to answer the world with less confusion. ||[noble]An amulet of fair and lucid making, in which grace seems not merely sharpened but ennobled. It heightens the inward light by which the Children of Ilúvatar perceive what is hidden, and gives the sense of a spirit more nearly attuned to clean song and truth.
[neutral]A finely worked amulet lends poise to thought and sharpens the inner senses. ||[noble]Its clear workmanship strengthens the wearer's grace and awareness.

[neutral]An amulet of green and gold, made with the thought of healing and the body's ready mending. It favours flesh that knits cleanly and weariness that passes sooner, as though the wearer were helped by a wholesome and well-ordered craft. ||[noble]An amulet in which the tokens of leaf and gold seem touched by a more ancient blessing. Under its care hurt closes with a swifter and gentler mercy, as though the gift of life itself had been remembered and renewed.
[neutral]Green and gold mark an amulet that helps the body mend and recover. ||[noble]A carefully finished healing charm encourages wounds to close more swiftly.

[neutral]An amulet made to husband the wearer's strength, keeping body and spirit from needless loss. It has the air of a traveller's or householder's safeguard, contrived so that health, heart, and even the store of food are spent more slowly. ||[noble]An amulet of older and more deliberate craft, preserving its wearer from the wasting of body and spirit with something like an ancient courtesy. It sustains health and grace alike, and makes even the long road seem less eager to consume what is good.
[neutral]A conserving charm slows the waste of health, spirit, and food. ||[noble]Its patient craft sustains body and grace through the demands of a long journey.
An amulet of dark iron, cold to the touch. It opens the wearer's sight to things hidden and unseen, but at a price: the dreams that come with it are not wholly of this world.
Cold dark iron frames a charm that reveals hidden things. The insight brings troubling dreams along with it.

[neutral]An amulet bearing the likeness of an open eye, made for watchers, scouts, and any who mistrust the dark's deceits. It sharpens sight and steadies the mind against illusion, as though its maker had spent long years learning how the Enemy's servants mislead the wary. ||[noble]An amulet whose open eye is wrought with a clearer and more solemn intent, as though watchfulness itself had been set to guard the wearer. Under it, false seeming and sorcerous trickery are less able to prevail against a mind resolved in cleaner light.
[neutral]An open eye marks a watcher’s amulet that sharpens sight against illusions. ||[noble]Careful engraving strengthens the clarity with which the wearer resists deceptive appearances.

An amulet of dull grey metal, stamped with a brand of thralldom from Angband's slave-pits, where countless Elves and Men were broken to labour in the sunless dark. Those who survived were hardened beyond reckoning, their bodies inured to every suffering—yet their spirits were diminished, worn to shadow by years without hope or the memory of stars.
A dull grey labour tag bears the number of a sealed Karth work gang. It hardens the body against suffering while diminishing the spirit.

An amulet of dull black stone, worn by the spies and scouts of Morgoth who crept through the passes of the Ered Gorgoroth under cover of night. The bearer moves as a shadow among shadows, silent and unseen—yet a faint dimming of the light clings ever to the wearer, as to all things that have dwelt too long in the service of the Enemy.
A dull black stone was issued to scouts travelling through ruined service passages. It aids silent concealment, but dims the light around its wearer.

An amulet of tarnished bronze, bearing the angular mark of one of Morgoth's war-captains. It lends a dull readiness for war: the hand strikes surer, and the body is warded against common blows. Yet the spirit coarsens under its influence, for it was wrought for creatures whose makers had no thought of grace nor beauty.
Tarnished bronze bears a military captain's angular seal. The charm steadies attacks and guards against ordinary blows while coarsening the wearer's spirit.

Wrought by the deep-smiths of Nogrod for the gatharim, those few masters who dared the uttermost shafts beneath the Blue Mountains where no light had shone since the making of the world. It fills the body with the endurance of living stone and wards the eyes against the sudden blinding flare of subterranean fire and the sorcerous dark alike. Only a handful were ever made, for the craft was costly and the delvers who needed them fewer still.
Deep-shaft crews carried this charm where sudden flares and unnatural darkness could blind a worker. It strengthens endurance and protects sight.

Fashioned by the jewel-smiths of Gondolin, where the memory of Valinor was most perfectly preserved in Middle-earth. These were given to the very few captains whom Turgon sent beyond the Encircling Mountains on desperate errands: each held something of the peace of that hidden city, a light against the terror of the outer world. The wearer's spirit is deepened and brightened, and no dread of the Enemy can shake the heart while it is worn.
A refuge workshop made this amulet for messengers crossing the storm barriers. It deepens grace and steadies the heart against fear.

[neutral]A ring of dark gemstone that seems to hold whispers within it. It sharpens the wearer's perception and reveals the hidden nature of things, as though it had long been used by those who searched out veins of ore, flaws of temper, and the concealed workings of craft. ||[noble]A ring of subtler and more lucid virtue, in which hidden knowledge feels less stolen than rightfully uncovered. It opens the eye to metals and craftwork with a patient clarity, as though old wisdom rather than mere suspicion had been set in the stone.

[neutral]A dark gemstone sharpens perception and helps uncover the hidden nature of materials and crafted objects. ||[noble]Clear-cut facets give the seeker a patient understanding of metal and workmanship.

A ring wrought in the fashion of the Dwarven-smiths of Ered Luin, the Blue Mountains, where the great cities of Belegost and Nogrod once stood. The Dwarves of those cities were renowned for their stubborn courage in the face of Morgoth's terror, and a measure of that endurance lingers in this ring.
Rugged workshop marks identify a ring made for crews in the Cleft Ranges. Its enchantment lends stubborn endurance against terror.

[neutral]A ring of subtle craft that quickens the wearer's instinct for danger. In battle, blows seem to pass a hair's breadth wide, as though long practice and a wary heart had been taught to the body through the finger that bears it. ||[noble]A ring of finer and fairer subtlety, turning danger aside with something like grace rather than mere alarm. Under its influence the body yields and recovers cleanly, as though guided by an unseen courtesy instead of naked fear.
[neutral]A subtle ring quickens the body's response to an approaching blow. ||[noble]Fine shaping lends a controlled ease to evasive movement.

[neutral]A bright amulet set with a ward against bodily harm. It has the look of a practical safeguard, prized by those who must trust charm and craft together when fang and blade come too near. ||[noble]A bright amulet whose ward is laid with uncommon purity, so that protection feels less like a barrier forced into place than like a clean refusal of malice. Under it, the violence of fang and blade is more gently and more surely turned aside.
[neutral]A bright charm wards the body against fangs and blades. ||[noble]Careful setting strengthens the amulet's protection against physical harm.

[neutral]A ring wrought to fortify the sinews of its wearer. It has the plain worth of a thing made for labour and battle alike, helping the hand to bear weight, draw hard, and strike with greater certainty. ||[noble]A ring in which strength has been ordered rather than merely increased. Under it, the arm feels not brutal but well-governed, as though force had been brought into the service of discipline, defence, and steadfast deeds.
[neutral]A practical ring fortifies the sinews for labour and battle. ||[noble]Its refined enchantment gives the arm strength without sacrificing control.

[neutral]A ring of delicate craft that lends nimbleness to the wearer. The hand grows quick and sure, and the body answers the will with a swiftness beyond its wont, as though old stiffness had been carefully unbound. ||[noble]A ring of finer grace, in which nimbleness is joined to measure. Under it the hand is not merely faster, but cleaner in its answer, and the body moves with something of the bright ease that lesser craft can only imitate.
[neutral]A delicately made ring lends speed and precision to the body. ||[noble]Fine craft gives the hand a particularly measured nimbleness.
A ring of pale blue stone, cold as the winds of Himring. Its chill provides protection against the flames of the Enemy.
A pale blue stone is cold against the finger. Its chill protects the wearer from fire.
A ring that glows with a gentle heat, as though it remembered the light of the Blessed Realm. Its warmth shields the wearer from the bitter cold of the north.
Gentle heat lingers within the ring's band. It shields the wearer against cold.

[neutral]A ring that steadies the hand and sharpens the eye. In battle, the wearer's strikes fall truer, finding the gaps in armour and guard with the sureness of a well-schooled hand. ||[noble]A ring whose exactness is touched by a cleaner mastery. Under it, aim feels less like narrow calculation than like a just line found and held, so that hand and eye agree with unusual certainty.
[neutral]This ring steadies hand and eye so attacks strike more accurately. ||[noble]Its finely adjusted enchantment brings aim and movement into unusually clear agreement.

[neutral]A ring of curious craft that seems to loosen the bonds upon the wearer. It has the look of a thing much valued by travellers and warriors alike, for it resists hindrance, numbness, and the body's unwilling stillness. ||[noble]A ring whose freedom is of a higher temper, resisting not only the body's stiffness but the imposed check of hostile will. In the Elder Days, such a thing would have been of great worth to those who stood against the binding malice of Morgoth.
[neutral]A curious ring resists numbness and imposed stillness. ||[noble]Its enchantment helps the wearer remain free of hostile bindings.
A ring of tarnished iron. It inflicts a creeping dread upon its wearer, driving them to flee from danger - though in their haste, they find themselves strangely nimble.
Tarnished iron carries a creeping dread that urges flight from danger. The same anxious urgency makes its wearer unusually nimble.

A ring bearing the brand of Bauglir, a name of the Dark Lord. Said to have been worn by the captains of his vanguard, it grants a fierce and devouring strength, but the wearer is afflicted by a hunger that the food of the earth cannot sate.
The regent's vanguard seal marks a ring that grants fierce strength. Its wearer pays with a relentless hunger.

[neutral]A ring set with a pale green stone that wards against venom. It looks like the sensible possession of hunters, delvers, and healers who know too well the bites and stings that lurk in dark places. ||[noble]A ring set with a pale green stone of cleaner virtue, seeming made not merely against common poison but against the special malice of the Enemy's creatures. The bite of wolf, spider, and fouler thing is more readily denied to one who wears it.
[neutral]A pale green stone wards against poison from bites and stings. ||[noble]A carefully set green gem strengthens the ring's defence against venom.

Forged in the ceaseless fires of Angband beneath the peaks of Thangorodrim, this ring of black iron shields its bearer from the fiercest flames. Yet it binds the wearer's flesh so deeply to the furnace that the mere touch of frost becomes a crippling agony, drawing the bitter cold of Utumno straight to their heart.
Black iron still holds the temper of the weather engine's furnaces. It grants strong protection from fire while making cold far more dangerous.

Hewn from pale stone as cold as the eternal ice that entombed the ruins of Utumno, this ring wards its bearer against the cruelest frosts of the North. Yet it plunges the wearer's blood into such an unnatural winter that the fires of Angband find them utterly defenseless, searing them with magnified fury.
A pale stone preserves a chill drawn from Karth's failed cooling chambers. It protects strongly against cold while leaving the wearer dangerously vulnerable to fire.

A ring of crude iron, stamped with the rune of Angband. Orc-captains wore such rings to master their companies by brute force alone. The strength it grants is real enough—yet the spirit withers under its influence, for it was made without art and without love.
Crude iron bears a military control stamp. It increases bodily strength while weakening grace.

A ring set with a dim red stone, given to the thralls who kept watch in the dark passages of Angband for spies and intruders. It sharpens the senses beyond their wont—yet the hunger of the pits gnaws ceaselessly at the wearer, as it gnawed at those who first bore it in the darkness beneath the mountains.
A dim red stone sharpens the senses for a long underground watch. Its enchantment also brings a persistent, gnawing hunger.

A crude ring of blackened bone, issued in great numbers to the thralls and lesser orcs who toiled in the breeding pits of Angband. It wards against the venom of the foul things that lurk in the dark, yet it was wrought with malice; it instills a craven fear in the wearer's heart, ensuring they remain ever subservient to the will of their cruel masters.
Blackened bone forms a cheap poison ward issued to the breeding crews. It also inflicts fear, keeping its wearer anxious and submissive.

A ring of cold iron, graven with runes of command in the Black Speech of Angband. The will of the Dark Lord echoes faintly within it—the wearer's resolve grows unyielding as stone, and fear itself recoils from them. Yet the ring's malice radiates outward like a burning brand, and all creatures nearby are roused to fury by its presence.
Command marks cover a cold iron band commissioned for the regent's officers. It strengthens resolve and repels fear, but rouses nearby creatures to anger.

A ring of dark stone that hums with a low and ceaseless voice, as of fell chants sung in the deeps of Angband. The bearer's voice gains a strange and terrible power - yet the dead are drawn to the sound from the dark places, and a creeping dread follows wherever the ring is worn.
Dark stone hums with a low, constant note. It empowers the wearer's voice while attracting the dead and bringing a creeping dread.

A ring of green and gold, fashioned in the manner of the Laiquendi, the Green Elves who dwelt in the deep woods of Ossiriand. It grants the quiet skill of the forest hunters: swift of step and keen with the bow.
Green and gold distinguish a hunter's ring from the wooded tide settlements. It favours a swift step and skilled archery.

Wrought by Curufin son of Fëanor, greatest smith among the living Noldor, for the hunters who guarded the Pass of Aglon under his brother Celegorm the Fair. Those scouts tracked Morgoth's servants through the tangled vales of Nan Dungortheb, where the brood of Ungoliant spun webs of bewilderment upon the unwary. The ring keeps hand and eye in perfect accord and the mind clear of all confusion, so that no sorcery may cloud the wearer's purpose.
A surveyor's ring aligns hand and eye while keeping thought clear. It protects the wearer against confusion.

Forged by the war-smiths of Belegost for the chosen guard of Lord Azaghal, who alone among the Free Peoples could face the fire-drakes and hold their ground. Each ring was a mark of rank, given when a warrior was admitted to that grim company and reclaimed when he fell. It fills the arm with the strength of the mountains and steadies the senses against even the most crushing blow, so that the bearer may stand where others would be broken.
Workshop guards once reclaimed this ring from each fallen member of their company. It strengthens the arm and steadies the senses against stunning blows.
A staff imbued with the power of binding, echoing the great doors and gates that were shut against Morgoth's hosts in the wars of Beleriand. It may shut and lock all doors in line of sight.
A binding staff can shut and lock every door in line of sight. Its design belongs to the old emergency containment crews.
A gem imbued with the power to undo locks and reveal what is hidden. It reveals doors and traps in line of sight and may open or destroy them.
This unlocking gem exposes doors and traps in line of sight. It can open or destroy them.

A gem that holds a captured radiance, releasing it in a brilliant flash when called upon. It lights up an area with a radius of 7 squares, plus the entire room if you are currently in one. This stuns any light-sensitive creatures within the area of effect.
A stored flash lights a radius of 7 squares and, if you stand in a room, the entire room. Light-sensitive creatures caught in the illumination are stunned.
A gem blessed with the virtue of cleansing, able to lift the taint of dark enchantments. It can cleanse one chosen item from your equipment, pack, or the floor, lifting curses where it can.
A cleansing gem can remove curses from one selected item in your equipment, pack, or on the floor. Some bindings resist its power.
A gem that reveals the hidden nature of things, granting knowledge as the loremasters of old possessed. It identifies an item. (This may be aborted without using up a charge.)
A diagnostic gem identifies the nature of a selected item. Cancelling the selection consumes no charge.
A gem that pierces the veil of darkness and stone, laying bare the paths around you. It reveals your surroundings.
This survey gem reveals the surrounding layout through darkness and stone. It was designed to recover routes when the engine's passages changed.
A gem attuned to the works of craft, that senses the presence of wrought things near and far. It shows you the whereabouts of all items on the level.
A searching crystal locates every item on the current level. Its response follows worked objects and loose possessions alike.
A gem that senses the presence of living creatures, be they friend or foe. It shows you the whereabouts of all monsters on the level.
A tracking crystal reveals the positions of all monsters on the level. Distance within the level does not hide them from its survey.
A staff bearing an enchantment of deep weariness, akin to the drowsing spells woven in the Elder Days. It causes a great weariness in all monsters in line of sight.
A fatigue staff burdens all monsters in line of sight with deep weariness. Its old containment fitting is worn smooth.
A staff that channels a commanding presence, echoing the terrible majesty of the great lords of the Elder Days. It causes fear in all monsters in line of sight.
A command staff instils fear in all monsters in line of sight. Its pulse carries the force of an overwhelming presence.

A gem of inward sight, turning the bearer's perception upon themselves. It shows all of your status effects and character traits. While diseased, it identifies the disease name and cure herb if you have Alchemy. Without Alchemy, each use has a 50% chance to identify the disease name; once the name is known, each use has a 50% chance to identify the cure herb. Discoveries last for the current infection and are saved. A new infection gets a new name and cure and resets them. Each use also gives a chance to reveal one active curse. Also shows how many diseases you are immune to for this run.

This diagnostic gem displays your status effects and character traits and may reveal one active curse with each use. During disease, Alchemy reveals both its name and cure herb; otherwise each use has a 50% chance to learn the name, then a 50% chance to learn the cure once the name is known. Findings persist in saves for that infection, but a new infection assigns a new name and cure and resets the discoveries. It also shows the number of diseases you are immune to for this run.

A gem imbued with the power of protection, in the manner of the ancient wards set upon the borders of Doriath. It can be used to create glyphs of warding, which your opponents have difficulty crossing.
A barrier gem inscribes glyphs of warding on the ground. Opponents have difficulty crossing the marks.

A light-absorbing gem darkens a radius of 7 squares and, if you stand in a room, the whole room. For that round's stealth checks, add your Will to stealth.
A horn whose dreadful note strikes fear into the hearts of those who hear it, as the horns of the Noldor once rang in the passes of the north. Its sound brings terror to your enemies.
A harsh horn note spreads terror among your enemies. Its mouthpiece bears the dents of hard service.
A horn whose blast rolls like thunder through the halls, dazing all who stand against you. Its sound stuns your enemies.
A thunderous horn blast stuns your enemies. The sound reverberates through enclosed passages.
A horn whose mighty blast hurls foes back like a gale from the mountains. Its sound blows your enemies back.
A forceful horn blast drives your enemies backwards. Its note strikes like a sudden gust.

A horn of terrible power, whose voice can crack the works of stone as the trumpets of the Valar shattered the pillars of Utumno. Its sound can shatter stone. In addition to the compass directions, brave souls can aim it up (u, or c with hjkl movement) or down (d).
This horn's blast can shatter stone. Aim in a compass direction, upwards with u (or c with hjkl movement), or downwards with d.
A horn that draws the attention of all nearby, for good or ill. It rings out a challenge to your foes.
A warning horn rings out a challenge that draws your foes' attention. Its signal is meant to be impossible to overlook.

A cordial of surpassing virtue, said to be in the manner of the healing drink of the Valar in the Blessed Realm. It cures stunning, confusion, hallucination, poison, blindness, and fear. It halves any current bleeding, restores 20 health and 20% of your maximum health, and restores all your voice. It also cures disease and restores all attribute points lost to that disease. Curing disease grants immunity to that disease for this run.

Spring cordial cures stunning, confusion, hallucination, poison, blindness, and fear, and halves bleeding. It restores 20 health plus 20% of maximum health and all voice; it also cures disease and restores every attribute point lost to that disease. A successful disease cure grants immunity to that disease for the rest of this run.

A foul brew distilled in the pits of Angband, thick and black and burning to the throat. The orcs of Morgoth drink it before battle to dull their pain and steel their craven hearts. It banishes all fear, restores 6 health and 8% of your maximum health, and stuns you (for 2d4 turns).
A thick black fighting liquor burns the throat, banishes fear, and restores 6 health plus 8% of maximum health. Its numbing shock stuns the drinker for 2d4 turns.

A potion infused with the waters of the Esgalduin, a river that flows through the hidden realm of Doriath beneath Melian's enchantment. It grants a bonus of +10 to perception for 20d4 turns, and restores a quarter of your voice.
A clear survey draught sharpens perception by +10 for 20d4 turns. It also restores one quarter of your voice.
A draught that clears the mind, lifting the fog of bewilderment and the daze of stunned wits. It cures stunning, confusion, and hallucination; and ends your rage.
A clarifying draught cures stunning, confusion, and hallucination. Its calming action also ends rage.

A draught of potent healing, brewed with the virtue of herbs and ancient craft. It halves any current bleeding and restores 15 health and 16% of your maximum health. It also cures disease and restores all attribute points lost to that disease. Curing disease grants immunity to that disease for this run.

A concentrated healing draught halves bleeding and restores 15 health plus 16% of maximum health. It cures disease and returns all attribute points lost to that disease. A successful disease cure grants immunity to that disease for the rest of this run.
A draught that renews the power of song, restoring what weariness and sorrow have spent. It renews your voice.
A singer's draught replenishes spent voice. It is prepared for speakers and performers whose breath must last through difficult work.

A draught that opens the inner eye, granting sight beyond the deceptions of Morgoth's servants. It restores your sight and enables you to resist blindness, resist hallucination, and see invisible creatures for 10d4 turns.
A revealing draught restores sight and grants resistance to blindness and hallucination. It also lets you see invisible creatures for 10d4 turns.
A draught brewed against the venoms of the Enemy's creatures. It cures any current poisoning.
An antidote neutralizes all current poisoning. Its bitter preparation is meant for immediate use after exposure.
A draught that hastens the body, lending a burst of speed to limb and sinew. It makes you move more quickly (+1 to speed) for 10d4 turns.
A stimulating draught increases speed by +1 for 10d4 turns. The body moves with a sudden burst of quickness.
A draught that steels the body against the extremes of fire and cold. It grants you temporary resistance to fire and cold for 20d4 turns.
A protective draught grants resistance to fire and cold for 20d4 turns. It prepares the body for both extremes of temperature.
A draught that quickens the sinews and fills the limbs with the vigour of youth renewed. It grants a bonus of +3 to strength for 20d4 turns, restoring strength in the process.
A strengthening draught restores strength and then grants +3 strength for 20d4 turns. Its concentrated preparation quickens the muscles.
A draught that sharpens the reflexes and lends a dancer's grace to hand and eye. It grants a bonus of +3 to dexterity for 20d4 turns, restoring dexterity in the process.
A reflex draught restores dexterity and then grants +3 dexterity for 20d4 turns. It lends precision to hand and movement.

A draught that hardens the body against weariness and hurt, steeling flesh and bone as iron is tempered in the forge. It grants a bonus of +3 to constitution for 20d4 turns, restoring constitution in the process.
An endurance draught restores constitution and then grants +3 constitution for 20d4 turns. The body is fortified against fatigue and injury.

A draught imbued with the light of elder days, that kindles the spirit and deepens the bond between the drinker and the unseen currents of the world. It grants a bonus of +3 to grace for 20d4 turns, restoring grace in the process.
An attuning draught restores grace and then grants +3 grace for 20d4 turns. It clears the inner senses.
A draught tainted with a sluggish curse. It slows you down (-1 to speed) for 10d4 turns.
A sluggish draught reduces speed by 1 for 10d4 turns. Each movement becomes harder to begin.
A draught laced with venom, deadly to the unwary. It causes 5d4 points of poison.
A venomous draught inflicts 5d4 points of poison. The liquid is unsafe to drink.
A draught cursed with the darkness of the Enemy. It induces blindness for 10d4 turns.
A darkening draught blinds the drinker for 10d4 turns. Its harmful effect closes off ordinary sight.
A draught that clouds the mind with bewilderment. It induces confusion for 5d4 turns.
A bewildering draught causes confusion for 5d4 turns. The drinker's thoughts lose their order.
A draught that numbs the limbs and dulls the reflexes. It reduces your dexterity by one point.
A numbing draught reduces dexterity by one point. The hands become clumsy and uncertain.
A draught that dims the spirit and severs the inner connection to the deeper currents of the world. It reduces your grace by one point.
A disrupting draught reduces grace by one point. It dulls the drinker's inner awareness.

A small wooden chest, plain and serviceable, such as a traveller, householder, or petty captain might use for coin, letters, and keepsakes. Its boards are worn by long handling, and it promises little beyond what it holds. Even so, the items within tend to be of good quality.
Worn wooden boards enclose a small storage chest. Its contents tend to be of good quality.

A small chest bound in steel, made to resist rough hands and the wear of hard roads. Such coffers were kept for coin, seals, and other things a prudent keeper would not trust to wood alone. The items within tend to be of great quality.
Steel bindings reinforce a small travelling coffer. Its contents tend to be of great quality.

A little casket adorned with bright stones and cunning metalwork. It has the look of a gift from some richer hall, or of a lord's keepsake-box, made for treasures too small to bear openly and too precious to neglect. The treasures within tend to be of superb quality.
Bright stones decorate a small, carefully worked casket. Its treasures tend to be of superb quality.

A large wooden chest with a stout lid and broad sides, fit for the storing of garments, household gear, or a wanderer's gathered wealth. A heavy steel chest has room for several items. They tend to be of great quality.

A lordly coffer overlaid with bright metal and gems, wrought less for burden than for display. Largest of its kind, it holds several treasures, and those within tend to be of superb quality.
Gems and bright metal cover the largest type of coffer. It holds several treasures that tend to be of superb quality.

A gift wrapped with uncommon care in bright cloth and cord. Its outward cheer sits strangely in the dark places of the world, and for that very reason it stirs a little wonder concerning the hand that prepared it. Whatever lies within is sure to be of superb quality.
Bright cloth and a carefully tied cord surround a gift. The contents are guaranteed to be of superb quality.

A small flask of lamp oil, carried by those who venture into the lightless halls beneath Angband, where even Elven eyes find no gleam to guide them. It goes into your supplies as an oil container, using one of four oil slots and holding up to 2,500 turns of light.
A small flask carries oil for underground lighting. In supplies it occupies one of four oil slots and holds up to 2,500 turns of light.

Small pieces of pale lumesilver are malleable, bright, and resistant to tarnish. At a forge they can be made into lumesilver items or alloyed into them.

A torch hewn from the wood of the mallorn, the golden trees that grow in the Blessed Realm and in the Elven havens of Middle-earth. It begins with 100 turns of light, can hold up to 200 turns, and only starts to sputter when 10 turns remain.

Dense fragments of fallen star metal are stronger than common steel. At a forge they can be made into star-iron items or alloyed into them.

Large, uneven letters march across the parchment: "There was a green great dragon. He lived beneath a hill, and there was no knight brave enough to knock upon his door." Below, a dragon has been drawn much larger than the hill. The writer has squeezed the door in afterwards.
A trainee's oversized handwriting records the opening steps of a tide-gauge inspection. Beside the instructions, an enormous valve has been drawn with a handle too small to turn.

A smaller, steadier hand has written in the margin: "A great green dragon, dear. The words must go in that order." Two curved marks exchange the offending words. Nothing has been said about the dragon, the hill, or the absence of a sufficiently courageous knight.
A careful supervisor has corrected the order of the inspection steps in the margin. The drawing of the impossible valve has escaped comment.

The large letters return, pressed so hard that the nib has almost pierced the parchment: "But why? He was green before he was great." Beneath this stands a very small dragon, carefully shaded green. Beside it is the same dragon, now too large to fit upon the leaf.
The trainee has pressed a reply so hard into the sheet that the nib nearly pierced it. Two diagrams argue that checking the handle first would have saved everyone trouble.

Here the story gives way to columns of curious words. Some have been crossed out; others are joined by branching lines. Along the bottom, in the first uncertain hand, is written: "If these words will not behave, perhaps I shall make some of my own." The dragon in the margin is asleep.
Inspection notes dissolve into columns of proposed abbreviations and branching arrows. At the bottom the writer declares an intention to invent a clearer notation.
Only one line has been written: "And when the dragon woke--" The rest of the scroll is blank. A heavy green scale holds the parchment flat, just below the place where the next word should be.
One line begins the final inspection report, then stops before naming the fault. A heavy metal washer pins the blank remainder flat.
