[shield]Its frame has been ordered with sober craft so that blows glance away from it more readily, and the bearer feels less naked beneath the enemy's weight. ||[greaves]The plates are shaped to take the hurt upon themselves, guarding shin and knee where a crippling stroke is often sought. ||[soft_armour]Hidden strength has been worked into it, so that the covering yields less quickly than its lighter fashion would promise. ||[mail]Link has been laid over link with a warding purpose, and the iron seems readier than common mail to hold against the press of war.
Reinforcement distributes the force of a blow across the covering. Its construction provides better protection than ordinary work of the same kind.

[robe]Its cloth has been steeped and stitched with clean things, as though healers had set their craft against venom and corruption. ||[soft_armour]Hide and cloth have taken some bitter ward against poison, after the fashion of hunters who expected fang, thorn, and tainted blood. ||[mail]The rings have been treated with preserving salts and sharp herbs, as if the harness were made for wars in foul airs and among poisoned wounds.
A treatment of salts and bitter herbs wards the wearer against poison. The protective preparation remains in the material.

[soft_armour]Though supple still, it has in it an inward endurance, as though the strange metal would spend itself last of all. ||[mail]The pale rings seem tireless in their joining, lending the wearer something of mithril's own unwearied strength.
Carefully joined metal lends the wearer endurance beyond its light weight. It is made to resist the fatigue of prolonged service.

[boots]These are made for the springy floors of ancient woods, and the foot feels less hindered by root, briar, or sudden need. ||[gloves]The hand keeps its freedom in them, ready for bowstring, branch, or blade without awkwardness or delay. ||[leather_armour]It recalls the green shadows of Brethil, where free hunters needed quiet movement and a body unbound by its own defence. ||[studded_armour]Even with its iron set upon it, this harness has been kept lithe enough for woodland fighting and swift going beneath trees.
Flexible construction leaves the body free to move. This is equipment for hunters who must turn quickly among roots and branches.

[robe]Its folds have been cut to hang close and quiet, swallowing small sounds that looser cloth would gladly betray. ||[leather_armour]The fastenings sit close and the hide does not creak as loudly as common armour when the wearer bends or turns. ||[studded_armour]Even the iron has been subdued as far as such gear may allow, so that it speaks less readily in dark places. ||[default]Its making favours silence, and it yields fewer sounds to stone, branch, or restless hand than such a thing should.
Close fittings and subdued surfaces reduce the sounds of movement. The workmanship favours stealth.

[shield]Boss, rim, and grip are joined with Nogrod's close cunning, so that the shield sits stout upon the arm without deadening hand, eye, or courage. ||[greaves]These plates have the exact poise of Nogrod, where even war-gear was fitted with a master-smith's pride. They steady the stride without stealing its readiness. ||[mail]Ring answers ring with Nogrod's rich exactness, and the harness seems made not only to endure blows, but to keep the warrior within it master of himself.
Precise workshop fitting keeps the wearer ready and composed within strong protection. Even small details were made to preserve control in battle.

[greaves]They are made for a planted stance upon stone, giving the legs a northern firmness that does not welcome retreat. ||[mail_corslet]This corslet has the stern honesty of northern smithwork, fit for warriors who were schooled to hold a line against terror. ||[hauberk]Long rings and iron discipline go together here, as though it had been prepared for chosen guards who would not easily be driven.
Stout construction favours a planted stance and firm resolve. It was designed for guards expected to hold their line under pressure.

[greaves]A memory of the cold uplands of Ladros clings to them, and the legs are better defended against bitter wind and frozen ground. ||[gauntlets]These iron-backed hands seem less troubled by cold, as if they had already known long watches beneath a hard northern sky.
A cold-weather ward protects the wearer during bitter winds and long watches. Its craft is practical equipment for exposed upland posts.

[boots]A sour corruption clings to them, as though they had long trod in foul pools and carried that taint away in the leather. ||[gloves]The touch they promise is unclean, fit to spread rot from hand to hand or from wound to wound. ||[default]Something sickly has entered its substance, and what should have sheltered the body now seems more likely to welcome corruption.
A sickly contamination has worked into the material. What should protect the body instead carries the threat of corruption.

[boots]The leather has been smoked dark after a cruel fashion, suited to stealthy feet abroad on ugly errands. ||[gloves]Black hide and soot-dark stitching give them the look of hands meant to grasp, throttle, and work unseen. ||[leather_armour]Its hide has been darkened almost to the colour of cinders, after the manner of prowlers who would pass half-lost in night and smoke. ||[studded_armour]Dark hide and black iron have been joined here in a hard and secretive fashion, more fit for ambush than open battle.
Soot-dark surfaces and black stitching conceal movement in smoke and shadow. The finish suits covert patrols and ambushes.

[mail_corslet]These links are roughly driven together after the orcish fashion, serviceable only because iron may endure bad hands. ||[hauberk]A long shirt of mail hammered out in some black forge, its strength bought at the cost of comfort, silence, and all grace.
Roughly joined black mail offers serviceable strength at the cost of comfort and quiet. It was produced for military issue with little regard for its wearer.
[shield]Its curve and binding have been tuned to spill the enemy's stroke aside, making the blow wander from its first intention.
The shield's curve and bindings guide incoming strokes aside. Its balance helps the bearer deflect a blow.
[shield]Rime-like virtue lies on it, and the hand behind the shield feels less threatened by heat, ash, and sudden tongues of flame.
A cold ward clings to the shield. It protects the hand behind it against heat and flame.
[shield]Rune is laid upon rune in the deep fashion of the Dwarves, and their mingled counsel abides here still, so that doom itself finds less easy passage through it.
Layered protective inscriptions cover the shield. Their combined wards make it harder for danger to reach the bearer.

[shield]It goads the bearer toward the harsh answer, as though a shield were given not for shelter but for driving into the thick of strife. ||[helm]A cruel temper has been worked into it, filling the mind beneath with heat, impatience, and a readiness to answer every slight in blood.
An aggressive enchantment fills the wearer with impatience and anger. Shelter becomes an invitation to push further into the fight.
[shield]The grave strength of Hithlum abides in it, as if it had been made for northern wardens who learned to hold fast beneath long war and colder skies than most men willingly remember.
This shield was built for an exposed northern watch, with strength to endure a long siege. Its temper favours standing firm under pressure.
[shield]It keeps the temper of the Blue Mountains, where the long roads between Nogrod and Belegost taught smiths to marry timber, iron, and patience into one strength without boast.
Timber and iron are joined with the patient skill of mountain road workshops. The shield's plain finish conceals unusually dependable strength.
[dagger]A memory of the first starlight of Cuiviénen rests in this small blade, making it seem fitter for a swift and graceful hand than for any coarse work of butchery.
A light, finely shaped dagger responds readily to a graceful hand. It rewards quick, precise movement.

[arrow]These shafts have the white and deadly neatness of Gondolin, as though fletched for the walls before dawn when the plain below was dark with orcs. ||[polearm]It bears the ordered wrath of Gondolin's gate-wards, who met troll and Balrog in the killing-space before the Hidden King's walls. ||[sword]Its edge keeps the cold bright pride of Gondolin, and wakes most fiercely where orc or rauko would profane fair craft. ||[default]The hidden city's high wrath lives in it still, and the servants of Morgoth are answered first.

[arrow]These neat shafts were prepared for service-gate defenders facing approaching orcs. ||[polearm]This weapon was issued to gate guards stationed against trolls and cinder fiends. ||[sword]Its edge was prepared especially against orcs and demons threatening the sealed service gates. ||[default]The weapon carries a gate defender's hostile purpose against the regent's servants.

[arrow]These shafts are feathered in the temper of Doriath's outer marches, where the wardens of Thingol slew wolf and spider before they came beneath the beech-shadows. ||[polearm]It has the watchful reach of a march-weapon from Doriath, made to keep fang and venomous web from the guarded woods. ||[sword]There is in it the grave beauty of Doriath under Melian's Girdle: quiet until the instant wolf or spider comes too near. ||[default]The Girdled Realm is remembered in it, and things of fang, fur, and venomous web are answered as trespassers.
Hunters guarding wooded tide channels commissioned this weapon. It is particularly effective against wolves and spiders.

[polearm]It has the long cold purpose of Nargothrond, where deep armouries were laid against wing, scale, and the blood-drinking night. ||[sword]A stern bright craft out of Nargothrond is in it, and the edge seems to remember dragon-fire and the stealth of vampires in dark places. ||[default]It keeps the hidden city's grim wisdom, prepared for dragon, vampire, and such elder evils as came prowling against Narog.
This weapon was made for crews facing the hazards of the abandoned upper chambers. It is especially effective against dragons and vampires.

[war_hammer]Its stroke feels appointed to lay troubling dead things back into silence, as a bell might end a long and evil echo. ||[polearm]It has the grave authority of a weapon meant to keep the restless dead at their proper distance and peace. ||[sword]A hush from the Halls of Mandos seems to rest along its edge, and the undead have little welcome in that memory.
A ward against the restless dead has been laid into the weapon. Its blows are meant to put those that rise again to rest.

[war_hammer]The stubborn fire of the Firebeards is in it still, fit for long labour at forge or in battle. ||[axe]It has the hot bright temper of a Dwarven forge, and the hand upon it seems less wearied by toil or battle. ||[mattock]Though a delver's tool, it has been wrought in the same fiery patience that served the Firebeards in their deepest works.
A furnace workshop gave this weapon a durable, tireless temper. It helps the wielder endure hard labour and battle.

[war_hammer]It carries the bold strength of Hador's House, and troll flesh seems especially hateful to its heavy blow. ||[glaive]Its long edge has the valour of the Men of Dor-lomin, eager for the great and brutish foes that once broke lesser lines. ||[axe]There is a man's fierce nobility in it, as though it had been borne by one who would rather die standing than yield ground to trolls. ||[sword]The proud war-spirit of Hador's House lives in its edge, and it is readier than common steel against the giant brood of darkness.
Its heavy striking surface was made for confronting trolls. The weapon favours a brave, direct stroke against such massive foes.

[war_hammer]It seems impatient even at rest, as though each blow had taught it to desire another before the first has finished falling. ||[glaive]Along its length there runs a battle-hunger that would carry the wielder too deep into the press if left wholly unchecked. ||[axe]It is eager for wide and ruinous strokes, despising prudence and all quiet measures of war. ||[sword]A rash and dangerous heat has entered it, and the hand that uses it may find wrath answering sooner than wisdom.
A dangerous eagerness drives the weapon from one attack toward the next. Its battle fury can carry the wielder beyond prudent limits.

[short_sword]It answers the hand with a bright fierce quickness, like one of those lesser blades that still carried the proud fire of Fëanor's house. ||[great_sword]Even in so great a blade there is a perilous swiftness, splendid and a little terrible, after the manner of the Fëanorians. ||[sword]A bright and restless mastery is remembered in it, noble in craft yet shadowed by the dangerous fire of Fëanor's line.
Unusual quickness runs through the blade, even where its size should make it cumbersome. Its craft encourages rapid, decisive swordwork.

[dagger]This knife has the look of a blade made to end speech at arm's length or less, before cry or struggle can fully rise. ||[curved_sword]Its cruel bend suits sudden slaughter in cramped places, where the stroke must be quick, filthy, and close. ||[short_sword]It is shaped for the first red instant of treachery, when a swift thrust matters more than any honour in the fighting.
A close-fighting blade is shaped for a sudden lethal opening. It suits a killer striking before a victim can raise an alarm.
[dagger]It seems meant for the off-hand and the second opening, a companion blade that works not alone but in cunning answer to another.
A companion dagger follows the main weapon's attack from the other hand. Its balance is meant for working in concert with a second blade.
[spear]A clear and exalted memory is in it, as though the Vanyar had taught its point to move beneath a cleaner light than Middle-earth now commonly knows.
A refined spear carries a clear and elevated enchantment. Its point answers a steady, purposeful hand.

[quarterstaff]This staff has the weathered virtue of Mithrim, like ash cut by the cold mere and seasoned through long exile. It suits one who must endure want without surrendering either lore or heart.
A weathered staff supports endurance through hunger and hardship. It belongs to the practical tradition of travelling scholars and displaced surveyors.
[quarterstaff]A bitter memory of the Grinding Ice clings to it, and the one who bears it seems schooled a little better for cold and want.
A cold-weather staff helps its bearer endure frost and want. Its fittings were made for crossing frozen, exposed ground.
[war_hammer]The whole weight of it is taught toward one blunt and ruinous purpose, fit to break guard, bone, or barred way alike.
The hammer's weight is concentrated into a blunt, battering stroke. It was made to break through resistance by force.
[war_hammer]Its head has a dreadful honesty: what it strikes, it means not merely to wound but to ruin.
A crushing head delivers a particularly destructive impact. Its purpose is to ruin what the blow reaches.

[spear]Its point longs for the straight deep road through mail and flesh alike. ||[great_spear]The weapon seems made to drive through a foe entire, with little patience for shields or lesser obstructions. ||[glaive]Even this broad blade has been taught a narrower cruelty, as though its sweep desired at the end to become a thrust.
A narrow attacking line gives the weapon a deep, armour-piercing bite. The point presses past the protection that would stop a broader stroke.

[curved_sword]This is the kind of blade an overseer might wear among lesser thralls: quick to threaten, eager to punish. ||[short_sword]It has the hard bullying temper of a captain set over slaves and orcs, ruling by nearness, noise, and fear. ||[spear]Its point is fit for keeping underlings at a distance and in obedience, while still promising sudden death. ||[glaive]The long blade has something of the drill-yard and the lash in it, meant to command space and compel submission. ||[axe]A brutal commander's axe, better suited to enforcement than to any generous trial of arms. ||[sword]A harsh authority clings to it, as though it had often been raised less against true foes than against those beneath command.
An overseer's authority clings to the weapon. It was carried to threaten underlings and enforce obedience at close range.

[curved_sword]Fire and black rage dwell in this crooked blade, after the fell manner of Udun beneath Thangorodrim. ||[great_sword]Its great edge seems to carry furnace-heat within it, as if drawn from some deeper and fouler fire than any honest forge. ||[axe]A heavy northern fire has entered it, making the stroke slower, fiercer, and more ruinous when it lands.
Furnace heat burns within the heavy weapon. Its slower, fiercer stroke brings fire to whatever it reaches.

[war_hammer]It has the cruel patience of Angband's deep forges, where strength mattered more than speed or mercy. ||[curved_sword]The black mountain's shadow seems on it, making even this crooked blade feel heavier with menace. ||[great_sword]A vast and joyless strength has been laid into it, like a weapon meant for the wars of Thangorodrim and nothing gentler. ||[axe]Its iron remembers smoke, pits, and labour without pity beneath the shadow of the triple peaks.
A deep-forge temper gives the weapon ponderous strength. Its weight and menace take precedence over speed.

[curved_sword]Dark and pitiless, it is a weapon for the slaughter of free folk, not for any honest proving of arms. ||[short_sword]The short black blade seems made for killing Men and Elves in the crush, where malice profits from closeness. ||[great_sword]Its long black edge carries the old hatred of Angband for the Children of Ilúvatar. ||[spear]This spear's point is set with a grim purpose toward the free peoples, as if black iron itself had learned enmity. ||[glaive]Along its edge there runs a hatred broad as the stroke it makes, cruelly bent toward Men and Elves alike. ||[axe]A black killing-tool for butcher's work among the free peoples. ||[default]Black iron and old malice are joined in it, and the Children of Ilúvatar are its favoured prey.
Black metal was prepared for deliberate killing of humans and elves. Its enchantment is especially hostile to those living targets.

[dagger]Its narrow edge has been blackened with venom for work done within a single breath, where whisper and wound must come together. ||[short_sword]Such a short blade takes poison readily to the press of sudden battle, turning a quick wound into a slower death. ||[curved_sword]Venom suits this crooked blade too well, for it was already half akin to the cruel fashions of the Enemy. ||[glaive]Even along so broad a reaping edge venom has been laid, adding lingering hurt to the first great stroke. ||[axe]The bit has been smeared with a bitter venom, so that even a glancing hew may fester after the blow. ||[default]Venom has been laid upon it after the manner of dark hunters and patient murderers.
Venom coats the attacking edge. Even a shallow wound carries harm beyond the immediate cut.

[dagger]Its weight gathers close to the hand, letting it turn like a thought and strike where the eye has only just marked the gap. ||[short_sword]It moves with the easy obedience of a well-matched companion, quick to recover and quick again to threaten. ||[axe]Though short and head-heavy, it has been poised so cunningly that the stroke falls clean without dragging the arm awry. ||[default]Weight and measure have been set with uncommon care, and the hand finds its true line in it almost at once.
Careful distribution of weight lets the weapon find its line and recover readily. It responds with uncommon balance to the wielder's hand.

[glaive]Its long blade has been ordered not only to strike but to hold ground, keeping danger a little farther from the bearer. ||[sword]There is a guarding temper in it, as though the blade had been taught to preserve as well as to wound.
The blade's balance favours guarding as well as striking. It helps the wielder turn danger away.

[dagger]It drinks too readily of any hurt it gives, as though the little blade had learned a hungering life of its own. ||[curved_sword]The crooked edge seems eager not merely to cut but to feed upon the hurt it makes. ||[spear]Its point goes forth like a leeching thing, coldly desirous of the life that runs behind skin and mail. ||[great_sword]Even so great a weapon has in it a starving will, and each wound seems to promise more than blood alone. ||[great_axe]This heavy blade carries a foul thirst, as though great wounds were prized chiefly for how much life may be drained through them. ||[default]A dark hunger abides in it, feeding on the life it spills.
The weapon feeds on life taken through its wounds. Its hungry enchantment draws more than blood from a successful strike.
[mattock]It was plainly made for the delving of hard places, and the bite of its iron seems eager for vein, seam, and buried gate.
A keen digging head is made for stubborn veins and hard stone. It improves the mattock's work in deep excavation.
[mattock]The grave strength of the Longbeards is in it still, fit for long delving where lesser folk would have laid tool and will aside.
A durable mattock supports strength through long sessions of digging. It comes from workshops that valued endurance as much as a sharp bite.

[mithril_helm]The pale metal takes light as still water takes stars, and gives it back with a clearer and more heartening fire. ||[great_helm]Even its stern face is kindled, so that the wearer seems to go crowned with a hard clear light amid the press of war. ||[helm]A clear brightness rests on brow and crest, and the darkness before the wearer is less lordly than it was.
A clear radiance gathers on the helm. Its light pushes back the darkness around the wearer.
[helm]Under it the mind gathers and hardens, refusing dread as a shield-wall refuses the sea. It remembers captains of the Free Peoples who would not bow, though the dark pressed close.
The helm strengthens resolve and helps the wearer resist dread. It was made for captains expected to remain steady under terrifying pressure.

[helm]Beneath it the shadows of the world are less able to deceive, and things hidden, veiled, or only half seen are more readily discerned. ||[light]Its light is of a clearer virtue than common flame, troubling deceit and making hidden things less willing to remain concealed. ||[default]Some clear virtue rests upon it that suffers little shadow or deceit.
A revealing enchantment helps the bearer see through concealment and deceptive shadows. Ordinary appearances have less power to hide what is present.
[helm]Thought runs cleaner beneath it, and the confusions of hurt, fear, and sorcery find less easy hold. A blow may still daze the flesh, but the mind is readier to master it.
The helm clears thought and steadies the mind against confusion. Its wearer can regain control more readily when hurt or hostile magic disrupts the senses.

[mithril_helm]Pale grace has been added to pale metal, so that the mind beneath it is lifted above coarseness and answers the world with a nobler measure. ||[lesser_jewel]Its light grows gentler and more lovely, and those who keep it near are reminded for a while of fairer things than dread.
A gentle enchantment heightens the bearer's grace. Pale metal or captured light carries the same quiet refinement.

[great_helm]Its face is shut behind a black visor, making of the wearer a dark and nameless threat whose gaze need not be seen to be feared. ||[helm]The brow has been darkened and drawn low, after the fashion of cruel captains who preferred menace to open countenance.
A dark visor conceals the wearer's expression behind a threatening face. Its lowered brow emphasizes menace over an open countenance.

[shield]Iron teeth stand from its rim, as if the bearer were meant to strike with shelter no less than with weapon, driving men back by brutality rather than skill. ||[great_helm]Spikes have been set upon it like a cruel crest, more fit to terrify thralls than to honour any valiant lord. ||[helm]A savage row of iron points has been added to it, proclaiming wrath and rough violence before the sword is ever drawn.
Projecting iron points turn protective equipment into a declaration of aggression. The cruel outline is meant to intimidate before combat begins.

[shield]It has the low cunning of the lesser orcs upon it, and seems made for snarling courage that fails unless there is a stronger master's whip behind it. ||[helm]A cringing malice clings to it, the temper of those small servants of Angband who are bold only when they outnumber the weak.
A cringing, spiteful enchantment marks equipment made for the lowest military ranks. Its courage depends too much on a stronger master nearby.
[cloak]Its weave drinks small sounds and its fall is close and wise, so that the wearer may pass by brush or broken stone with less betrayal from cloth and clasp.
Close weaving suppresses the small sounds of cloth and clasp. The cloak helps its wearer pass quietly through rough ground.

[robe]A gentle stored warmth abides in its folds, like memory of a hearth long tended against winter and ill weather. ||[cloak]It holds the body's heat with unusual kindness, a welcome companion on cold marches and beneath bitter stars.
Stored warmth lingers in the cloth. It protects the wearer during cold marches and exposed watches.
[cloak]Long roads and cold bivouacs are remembered in it; it wastes little, asks little, and keeps its strength for the leagues still to come.
A travelling cloak is prepared for long roads and cold camps. Its conserving craft helps the wearer keep resources for the journey ahead.

[robe]There is in it a dead coolness, and the cloth lies against the skin like shade that has forgotten the sun. ||[cloak]Its folds keep an unkind chill of their own, as though they had long hung in some lightless place where warmth never entered. ||[boots]Cold rises through them from stone and earth, numbing the step and making every road feel lonelier than it is. ||[gloves]They leach warmth from the hands little by little, until even a ready touch grows reluctant and uneasy.
An unnatural chill leaches warmth from the wearer. The material feels cold even where the surroundings should offer comfort.
[cloak]A red courage seems sewn into it, and the life in the wearer is less easily spilled away. Hurt finds a steadier heart within its folds than it would have found elsewhere.
A life-preserving ward steadies the wearer against the loss of blood. Its red stitching marks equipment made to keep an injured traveller alive.
[cloak]A memory of the Golden Flower of Gondolin abides in it, and with that fair device come bright courage and a grace that does not readily bow to fear.
A bright flower device accompanies a charm of courage and grace. The wearer is less easily cowed by fear.

A yew stave blackened by foul smoking and over-hard firing. It has the grim temper of a northern war-bow, fit for bitter wind, long waiting, and far shots loosed at quarry the archer has no wish to see close at hand.
Heavy smoking and harsh firing have blackened the yew stave. Its grim temper suits long waits and distant shots in bitter weather.

[shortbow]A bleak memory of Lammoth clings to it, where the Enemy's scouts ranged the echoing shore beneath wind and wolf-cry. It feels made to shoot first when peril breaks suddenly from mist or stone. ||[longbow]It has the far and joyless watch of Lammoth beneath the screaming coast-wind, fit for black sentries who marked danger early and loosed from afar across the empty strand.
A coastal scout's bow responds quickly when danger appears from mist or rock. Its design favours the first shot of a sudden encounter.

[dragonhorn_bow]Even the fell horn has been hallowed, and when the string is drawn a cleaner fire seems to answer the old. What was taken from a servant of Morgoth has been bent toward a brighter war. ||[bow]A pale virtue has been laid upon it, and bow and string seem readier to send light before them into dark places that love no clear ray.
A radiant enchantment accompanies the bow's shot. Clear light is turned against creatures that thrive in darkness.

[shortbow]It has the keen woodland vigilance of the Marchwardens, who kept green borders against creeping things and sudden trespass. In the hand it feels alert even at rest, as though little in brush or dusk could pass it wholly unseen. ||[bow]It bears the watchful temper of the Marchwardens, fit for a border guard who must read stir and shadow without yielding the heart to fear.
A border watch enchantment sharpens vigilance without yielding to fear. The bow suits a guard reading small movements at the edge of cover.

[dragonhorn_bow]Even this fell horn has been schooled to the grey patience of the Falas, as though sea-wind and salt had cleansed some part of its old dragon-fury and turned it toward watch upon the west. ||[bow]It keeps the clear far-seeing temper of the Falas, where mariners and shore-wardens watched the grey sea in cold winds, reading danger while it was yet only a speck between wave and sky.
A shore-watcher's bow favours keen sight across long distances. Its maker expected danger to appear first as a small movement on the horizon.

[dragonhorn_bow]Even the horn of a dragon has here been taught a fairer obedience, as though the sea-longing of the Falmari had drawn its old violence into a cleaner and more certain line. ||[bow]The memory of the Falmari is in it, and the shot seems to seek a truer course, like a white bird stooping cleanly above the sea.
Careful tuning gives the bow a truer line. Its shot follows the archer's intention with unusual accuracy.

[shortbow]A hush of Menegroth lies on it, where fair things were kept hidden beneath stone and beech. It seems fit for swift hunters and guards who passed between the Thousand Caves and the outer woods. ||[longbow]It bears the deep and guarded nobility of Menegroth, as though wrought for silent watches under beeches and for the king's own hunts, where the shaft flew far yet secrecy remained unbroken.
A hunting bow is tuned for concealed watches and silent movement. Its design suits patrols passing between underground shelters and wooded banks.

It remembers the Long Peace that followed Dagor Aglareb, when the bowmen of the north kept unwearied watch upon the Enemy's land. Its draw is patient and warlike, fit for a long line and for distant shots loosed before the threat could break into the open.
A siege-watch bow was made for patient, distant shooting. Its long service belongs to defenders who watched an approaching threat before it reached their line.

Its back has been stiffened with horn in a harsh northern fashion, giving the little bow a savage cast beyond what its size should bear. It seems made for strong-handed prowlers who value a sudden hard shot above any fair ease in the drawing.
Horn backing stiffens the small bow beyond the force its size suggests. The draw demands a strong hand.

This bow has the temper of the black hosts of Angband, quick to cast death into the first broken ranks of Men or Elves. One can almost hear in it the ugly shouting of musters and the trampling rush of cruel companies whenever the string is drawn.
A military bow is built to strike quickly as the first ranks of humans or elves break. Its harsh temper favours an abrupt, aggressive onset.
[arrow]Their heads are smeared with a bitter venom, so that even a shallow graze may carry the hunter's will deeper than the iron itself.
Bitter venom coats the arrowheads. A grazing hit can poison as well as wound.

[arrow]These shafts are headed with long narrow bodkins, made to seek the joins of mail and the lesser kindnesses of armour. They favour the hard straight shot that asks not for broad hurt, but for a single deep finding.
Long narrow bodkins seek the joints and weaknesses of armour. The shafts favour deep penetration over a broad wound.
[greaves]Moonlike radiance plays about them when darkness gathers, silvering the path at the wearer's feet and making the enemies of moonlight less eager to draw near.
A pale radiance surrounds the greaves in darkness. It lights the path and discourages creatures hostile to such light.
[boots]The leather gives little answer to stone or leaf, and even a hurried step keeps more of its counsel than such boots have any right to do.
Soft, quiet fittings keep the boots from announcing each step. They help preserve silence even when the wearer hurries.
[greaves]Their bright plates seem strangely free of catch or hindrance; root, wire, and cunning trap alike find it harder to hold the leg that wears them.
Smooth plates and a freeing enchantment make the greaves harder to catch. Roots, wires, and traps have more difficulty holding the wearer.
[boots]Once the stride is set, they seem to hunger for the next step, and the next again, until the road itself appears to yield more quickly beneath the wearer.
An accelerating enchantment carries the wearer's stride forward. The boots increase the speed of travel.
[boots]They gather calf, knee, and heart into one sudden spring, as though ditch, snare, or broken stone were only a question to be answered in a single bold motion.
The boots lend force to a sudden leap. They help the wearer spring across gaps and obstacles.
[greaves]Iron has been cruelly over-set upon them, turning each step into a ringing challenge. They are fit for harsh soldiery who mean to be heard coming and to trouble quieter hearts by the sound.
Excess iron makes each step ring out. These greaves suit an enforcer willing to sacrifice quiet for a threatening approach.

[boots]A false craft is in them, and the feet are tempted toward the uncertain stone, the hidden edge, and the way that looks easiest only from a little distance. ||[greaves]They seem made for black roads where danger is half the master's purpose, and the step is driven onward whether the ground is honest or no.
A treacherous enchantment draws the feet toward uncertain ground. Apparently easy routes conceal dangers the equipment makes harder to avoid.

[boots]They carry the memory of a long evil road, where marchers were driven north beneath whips and foul standards until even rest was forgotten. ||[greaves]There is in them the hard rhythm of Angband's marches, more suited to trampling obedience than to any free man's road.
The equipment carries the relentless rhythm of a forced march. Its harsh influence leaves little room for rest or quiet travel.
[gloves]They preserve the fingers from weather and string-burn without deadening them, and the bowstring seems to come away more cleanly beneath the hand.
The gloves protect against weather and string-burn while preserving the fingers' sensitivity. They make the release of a bowstring cleaner and more controlled.

[gauntlets]Even through iron there abides a strange healing quiet, turning the war-hand from mere wounding toward guarding and relief. ||[gloves]A cool and restful virtue is in them, as though the hands had been washed in the still waters of Lorellin and taught a gentler craft against hurt.
A healing enchantment settles in the hands. It favours care and recovery even within equipment made for fighting.

[gauntlets]Their joints are wrought for the sword rather than for the fist alone, preserving in iron the quick answer of a master's parry. ||[gloves]The fingers remember old discipline, and a blade held in them turns aside danger more readily, as though schooled by long practice in the guarded halls of the Noldor.
The hand protection is shaped for precise swordwork. It improves the quick, guarded response of a practiced parry.
[gauntlets]Their weight is grave but wholesome, filling the hand with the stubborn strength of iron and stone. Fine quickness is somewhat denied, yet the grip becomes hard to shake or weary.
Heavy construction fills the hands with strength and a firm grip. Fine dexterity suffers under the burden.
[gloves]Though light as high metal should be, they lend the hand a greater command, so that grip, lift, and stroke all seem to answer a deeper strength than flesh alone would provide.
A strengthening enchantment gives the hands greater force without adding the expected weight. Grip and stroke answer more strongly.
[gauntlets]Hooked iron has been added at fingertip and knuckle, so that the hand is turned from grasping toward rending. They are fit for cruel work at close quarters and little else.
Hooked iron projects from fingers and knuckles. The gauntlets are made to rend at close quarters.

[gauntlets]These plates are made for the faithless close-in stroke, seizing advantage where a nobler fighter would have held his hand. ||[gloves]The hand within them grows watchful for the turned back and the ill-guarded instant, after the fashion of those who strike only when honour has already been abandoned.
A treacherous enchantment favours attacking a turned back or an unguarded moment. The hands within seek an unfair opening.
[gauntlets]Every joint and edge is contrived for hurt that lingers. They were not made merely to master an enemy, but to make pain speak long after the blow has fallen.
Cruel joints and edges are built to cause lingering pain. These gauntlets were designed for deliberate torment.

[lantern]Its flame burns with a clearer and more searching light, driving the dark a little farther back from every crack and turning. ||[lesser_jewel]Its captive radiance has been opened a little more, and the jewel shines like a steadfast star in a deep place. ||[feanorian_lamp]The housed light within it has been drawn nearer to the bright intent of its makers, until its beam seems less earthly than wrought of remembered dawn.
The light source has been adjusted to release a brighter radiance. Its beam drives darkness farther away.
[lantern]The flame within will not wholly trust its own burning, but gutters, wavers, and breeds moving shadows that trouble the eye more than the dark would have done alone.
An unreliable flame gutters and wavers. Moving shadows make the lantern's light difficult to trust.

[curved_sword]Its edge has been hacked into cruel teeth that worry flesh more than they truly cut, after the manner of orc-blades from Angband. ||[sword]The long edge has been broken into savage notches, so that each stroke rends as well as bites. ||[axe]The blade has been left in brutal teeth, fit to tear mail-links and leave mangled wounds behind it. ||[glaive]Along its sweeping edge run ugly notches, turning each reaping stroke into a tearing one. ||[default]Its edge has been worked into cruel teeth more fit to rend than to cut cleanly.
Cruel teeth interrupt the weapon's edge. Its wounds tear where a smooth blade would cut cleanly.

[dagger]It has been lightened until it seems almost eager, ready in the fingers before the will has fully spoken. ||[sword]Though made for war, it answers the hand with an Elvish quickness rare in weapons of such reach. ||[spear]Its length has been made obedient, and the point comes to line with scarcely a thought. ||[axe]Its weight is drawn close and made strangely governable, so that even the recovery of the stroke is swift. ||[default]Craft has drawn out its needless burden and left behind a quicker, more willing thing.
Unnecessary weight has been removed from the weapon. Its quicker response makes it easier to turn and recover.

[amulet]A pale and wholesome radiance abides in it, like a memory of stars seen before the Sun. Under that clear influence the heart is less willing to yield to dark fancy, blind terror, or deceitful seeming.
Pale radiance surrounds the amulet. Its clear influence steadies the mind against terror and deceptive appearances.
[amulet]An unwholesome dusk hangs about it, as though the little thing withheld what light should naturally rest upon it. The eye slips from it, and the mind mislikes to dwell upon it long.
An unhealthy dusk clings to the amulet. It seems to withhold light and discourage close attention.
[ring]Something in it has been secretly marred. Its virtue remains, yet not cleanly: one feels a lurking warp in the work, as if help and harm had been brought too near akin within the circle.
A hidden flaw twists the ring's enchantment. Its useful power survives, but harm has been mixed into the work.
[ring]Some fair hallowing rests upon it, gentle as starlight on still water. It steadies the spirit, and from it there rises something of the inward peace from which true song is born.
A calming blessing rests on the ring. It steadies the spirit and supports the inward composure needed for song.

[mattock]The iron has been drawn hard toward the bite, and each stroke falls with the grave certainty of a delver breaking stubborn seam, root, or barred stone door. ||[war_hammer]More of its will has been gathered into the head, so that the blow seems to travel on after impact, troubling shield, mail, and bone together. ||[hand_axe]More weight has been laid into the bit, and the small axe now bites with a depth surprising in so short a weapon, as though meant to end the matter in one hard meeting. ||[battle_axe]More of its burden is laid into the edge, and once the stroke is loosed it comes down like a sentence, not lightly to be recalled. ||[great_axe]Its vast head is burdened further still, until the falling stroke seems fit to sunder timber, harness, and courage alike.
Extra weight has been concentrated at the striking end. The weapon delivers a deeper, more forceful impact at the cost of a heavier stroke.
[quarterstaff]There is an answering note hidden in the wood, and hand, voice, and breath come more readily into one accord, as though an old song slept in it and woke gladly when called.
A resonant note lives within the staff's wood. It helps hand, breath, and voice work in accord.
[war_hammer]An old furnace-memory abides in it, not spent by years or ash. When the hammer strikes, the hidden fire in the metal seems to wake again, as though the forge itself had judged the blow.
Stored furnace heat awakens when the hammer strikes. Fire accompanies its impact.

[dagger]This is the sort of knife a hunted man might trust in the wild: plain to hide, quick to cast, and ready alike for meat, rope, or a sudden foe in the thicket. ||[spear]It has the lean look of a weapon borne by hard wanderers, fit to take food in the wastes and keep wolf or orc at distance when the fire burns low. ||[hand_axe]Small enough for the belt and useful in camp as in ambush, it recalls the harsh craft of outlaws who lived by swift hands, keen eyes, and little mercy from the world.
A practical outlaw's weapon serves camp work, hunting, and a sudden fight. Its balance suits hard travel and a quick cast from cover.

[short_sword]Its edge is schooled to the green secrecy of Ossiriand, where the Laiquendi let leaf, shadow, and silence fight beside them; the stroke seems already gone before the enemy has found the hand.
The shortsword is tuned for close woodland ambushes. Its quick stroke works with concealment and silence.

[quarterstaff]Something of Tirion upon Tuna is in it still: the clear order of high speech, measured thought, and strength governed by lore. It answers hand and voice as if long accustomed to halls where wisdom and power were not wholly sundered.
A survey college's staff supports measured speech, ordered thought, and controlled strength. It answers the voice as readily as the hand.

[war_hammer]The dragon-war of Belegost is remembered in it, and the head seems taught for scale, plated neck, and the great bones beneath them. ||[hand_axe]Though small, it bears the old Dwarven cunning of Belegost, meant to find the seam beneath scale or the softer place behind the jaw of a great worm. ||[battle_axe]Its broad edge recalls the dragon-fighters of Belegost, who trusted a sure hewing stroke where scale and fire would have broken lesser hearts. ||[great_axe]A mighty axe of Belegost's stern tradition, fit to bite deep even where scale and sinew lie heavy over monstrous life.
The weapon was prepared for dragon-hunting crews. Its striking surface is made to find vulnerable places beneath scale and heavy bone.

[war_hammer]There is in it the memory of deep vaults where the folk of Nogrod met things with too many limbs and too little light, and learned to strike hard before terror could master the heart. ||[hand_axe]It seems made for the close and dreadful work of delving, where webs, narrow rock, and sudden horrors leave room for only one swift and certain blow. ||[battle_axe]Its edge recalls the black ways under Nogrod, where broad iron was prized for clearing web, limb, and nightmare alike from a crowded passage. ||[great_axe]A grave under-earth weapon, fit for those who went armed into the deep places of Nogrod where ancient horrors were better sundered outright than merely held at bay.
Deep excavation crews carried this weapon beyond the mapped passages. It is especially effective against spiders and horrors.

[war_hammer]A grave ward has been laid on it in the name of the Smith, and unclean things that move after death seem little welcome beneath its descending stroke. ||[hand_axe]Though small, it carries a stern hallowing, as if made to bite truly upon the deathless and the blood-drinking things that mock the works of living hands. ||[battle_axe]Its broad edge has in it a lawful wrath against the walking dead, as though the craft of Aulë denied them any lasting place in the world of stone and iron. ||[great_axe]A deep protective virtue abides in it, and even its vast stroke feels set not only to destroy, but to cast down what should have remained in darkness and silence.
A cleansing ward turns the weapon against undead and blood-drinking creatures. Its purpose is to end what should no longer move among the living.
[robe]This robe keeps the memory of hymns sung beneath Varda's stars, and around it fear and darkness seem for a while less lordly than before.
A courage-bearing chant has been woven into the robe. It helps its wearer challenge fear and darkness.
[robe]A hush of silver memory lies upon it, like dew beneath the last stars before dawn. In its keeping, sound and disquiet seem to fall away from the wearer.
A silvery enchantment quiets the robe. Sound and disturbance fall away around its wearer.

[leather_armour]It remembers low songs in echoing places, where the delvers of old learned the temper of stone by voice as much as by hand. Hidden ways yield themselves more readily to such music. ||[studded_armour]Even its iron seems tuned to the deep speech of rock, as though it had gone often through caverns where song was used in place of hammer or torch.
The armour is attuned to the resonant craft of underground surveyors. Songs reveal hidden routes through stone more readily.

[mail_corslet]Its rings are closed in the ancient manner of Belegost, where the Dwarves first brought ring-mail to its full mastery, each link measured, riveted, and laid for endurance. ||[hauberk]Long linked order runs through it, after the fashion of Belegost's mail-smiths, who made strength flexible and burden more evenly borne from shoulder to hem. ||[mithril_mail]Here the old ring-mail craft of Belegost is married to mithril, and the harness seems at once lighter, closer, and more sure than any common mail.
Small, securely closed rings distribute the armour's burden while maintaining strength. The workshop method makes protective mail unusually flexible and well fitted.

[dragonhorn_bow]Even this fell horn has been gentled to the hush of Sirion's Havens, where the last fair remnant kept watch beside grey water and hidden reeds. It seems made for a patient archer who must go lightly, lie still, and yet slip free the instant danger closes.
A quiet enchantment suits the bow to patient watches near water and reeds. Its bearer can remain concealed and slip free when danger closes.
[studded_armour]In it abides the hard vigilance of the Black Gate, where no footfall went unweighed and mercy was not known; it sharpens watchfulness, but breeds a cruel unrest in the wearer.
The armour carries a gate-watch ward that heightens vigilance. Its protection also breeds an oppressive restlessness.
[mail_corslet]Dust, ash, and the bitter wind of Anfauglith seem to abide in it still; it fares best where bodies crowd together in hard war, but leaves little room for quiet step or hopeful heart.
Heavy mail is fitted for crowded, sustained combat. It gives little consideration to stealth or the wearer's peace of mind.
[leather_armour]It remembers the crouching hunters that Morgoth sent abroad beyond his walls, and favours stealth that serves suspicion rather than courage.
The leather armour favours a crouching scout's quiet movement. Its dark patrol markings belong to forces sent to stalk and observe.

[greaves]They are shod for the brutal onset, after the manner of those hard legions that drove thralls and lesser soldiery before them. Their weight teaches a trampling stride, and the iron seems to desire not the hidden step but the sudden rush that breaks fear and order together.
Reinforced greaves favour a forceful charge. Their heavy stride sacrifices concealment for a sudden, trampling onset.

[boots]These are fit for the keeper of pits and barred ways, whose coming is known before he speaks. In them abides the gaoler's fell office: to force another from his place, to tread where he wills, and to leave a dread behind him in the dark.
A prison officer's boots impose a threatening presence. Their enchantment supports forcing another creature from its place.

[hauberk]It bears the merciless weight of those black companies that kept watch beside the Balrogs of Angband, teaching the wearer to stand like a wall at a dreadful master's side and to think little of pain.
A heavy guard's hauberk teaches the wearer to endure pain and hold position. It was made for companies stationed beside the furnace spirits.
[great_helm]Such a helm is meant to be seen above lesser soldiery, hardening the will of the one who wears it while driving all beneath him toward noise, fury, and blind obedience.
A commander's great helm strengthens the will of its wearer. Its influence also encourages noise and aggressive obedience.
[robe]Song has been turned awry in it, so that what should have joined hearts is bent instead toward mistrust, revelation against one's will, and the unmaking of quiet accord.
Discordant threads disrupt the cooperation of voices. The robe's enchantment turns song toward mistrust and unwanted revelation.

[shield]The memory of a foul banner and the bellowing charge around it clings to this shield; it is fit for a retreat kept under blows, but it carries with it the bully's will and the captain's harsh pride.
A military standard's harsh authority clings to the shield. It suits a withdrawal under attack while encouraging the bearer's domineering pride.

[arrow]These are cruel hunting-shafts, barbed for the long chase rather than the clean kill. One might think them fletched for the black hunts of the Enemy, when free folk or web-spawn were driven from cover by pain, shouting, and the promise of worse behind.
Barbed hunting arrows are made for a painful chase. Their heads are particularly deadly to humans, elves, and spiders.

[feanorian_lamp]A golden memory has been kindled in it, as though some last echo of Laurelin were housed within the crystal. It answers gladly to song, and when its radiance is lifted up the dark is thrust farther back, while creatures of shadow endure that light with pain and unwillingness.
Warm golden light fills the lamp's crystal. It responds to song with greater radiance that hurts creatures of shadow.
A once-stout helm fouled by rust and neglect, its rim eaten thin and its guard much reduced.
Rust has eaten the helm's rim and thinned its protection. Neglect has left a once dependable guard badly weakened.
Boots worn thin and loose, fit for the road only in dire need.
The boots are loose and worn thin. Their failing construction offers little help on a difficult road.
A shield cracked and splintered by some heavy stroke of old.
A heavy blow has cracked the shield's frame. Splintered wood interrupts the surface that should bear an incoming strike.
A blade whose edge is nicked and worn, diminished in bite.
Chips and wear spoil the blade's edge. Its damaged cutting surface bites less effectively.
A shortsword gone slightly out of true, its point and balance both spoiled.
The shortsword is bent out of line. Both point and balance have suffered.
A spear with a cracked shaft and a dulled head, still serviceable but poor.
A cracked shaft and blunt head weaken the spear. It remains usable, but performs poorly.
A shortbow left damp and untended until its limbs have lost their true cast.
Damp storage has warped the shortbow's limbs. Its draw no longer sends a shaft with a true cast.
A cloak in tatters, frayed at hem and shoulder and of little aid in concealment.
The cloak is frayed and torn at shoulder and hem. The ragged cloth offers little concealment.
Gauntlets with split leather and bent iron plates that no longer sit cleanly.
Split leather and bent plates spoil the gauntlets' fit. Their damaged joints no longer close cleanly.
Greaves hammered out of shape, their plates caved and their straps strained.
Impacts have caved in the greaves' plates and strained their straps. They no longer sit correctly on the legs.
[lantern]Its glass is cracked and its fittings bent awry, so that no steady light can be kept within it until a smith mends the hurt.
Cracked glass and bent fittings prevent the lantern from sustaining a steady light. A smith must repair it before it can serve properly.

[helm]The old war-pride of the Broadbeams abides in it still. Not merely dreadful, it is kingly in wrath, after the manner of Dwarf-lords who went masked into dragon-war, so that the enemy's courage failed before the stroke was ever given.
A commanding mask gives the helm a particularly fearsome presence. It was designed to shake an enemy's courage before the first blow.

[gloves]The pale metal has been wrought so cunningly that wrist and finger move almost as though they were unarmed. There is in them a swift and delicate obedience, rare in any hand-armour and rarer still in a defence strong enough to meet the stroke.
Precise articulation leaves wrist and finger unusually free. The hand remains agile within strong protection.

[robe]Its folds have been cut with a subtle craft, so that the body within seems to slip the enemy's full notice. It does not turn the stroke as armour does, but lets it go awry, as if cloth, step, and sudden turning had entered into quiet agreement.
The robe's cut supports quick turns and evasive steps. It helps the wearer avoid a blow rather than absorb its force.

[shield]Its frame has been pared down and the boss set close, so that it guards the arm without burdening the step. One who bears it can still weave and turn as freely as the unarmoured. ||[helm]It has been beaten thin and fitted near to the brow, sparing of weight where lesser smiths would pile on iron, so that the head stays light and the wearer quick to slip aside.
Careful thinning removes unnecessary weight from the protection. The wearer can turn and dodge with less burden.

[dagger]The Haladin learned knife-craft behind timber walls and beneath close boughs. Orcs pressed their stockades, the wolves of the Enemy ran with his raiders, and the spawn of Nan Dungortheb haunted their westward road. Their broad, short blades cleared web, flew quickly at a springing wolf, and found the joints of Orc-mail when fighting became too close for spear or bow.
A broad short dagger was designed for forest stockades and cramped defence. It clears webs, can be thrown quickly at wolves, and is especially deadly to orcs, wolves, and spiders.

[dagger]The thralls of Tevildo were watched by the great Cats of his household, while the wolves of Angamandi hunted those who fled. Denied all weapons, they altered the knives of kitchen and slaughter-house: stiffening the point so it would not turn on a wolf's ribs and weighting the blade for a sudden cast at a leaping Cat. To a gaoler's eye they remained tools; in a captive's hand, they became the first stroke of escape.
Captive kitchen workers modified this knife beneath their guards' notice. A stiffened point can meet a wolf's ribs, and its weight suits a sudden throw at a leaping hunting cat.

A ring of twinned serpents with emerald eyes meeting beneath a crown of golden flowers. Finrod Felagund gave it to Barahir after Barahir saved his life in the Dagor Bragollach, vowing eternal friendship between his house and Barahir's line. When Beren came to Nargothrond bearing this ring, Finrod honoured his oath even unto death. It is a token of the most faithful bond between Elves and Men in all the Elder Days.
Emerald-eyed serpents meet beneath golden flowers on this ring. The linked figures were the seal of a harbour cooperative, whose members pooled their stores when the tide gates failed.

A ring that once graced the hand of Melian, a Maia who dwelt in the gardens of Lórien before she came to Middle-earth and wedded Thingol in Doriath. Her power wove the Girdle that kept the realm hidden from all evil, and the ring holds an echo of her foresight.
A careful observer's ring once belonged to the keeper of a storm-isolated garden. Its enchantment preserves a measure of foresight and the watchfulness needed to maintain a hidden refuge.

A delicate necklace traced with intricate designs, once worn by Tinfang Gelion, the Piper, a mysterious spirit of the twilight woods. His flute-playing could bind even the nightingales to silence. To wear this amulet is to hear the echo of Elvish music and long for starlight.
Intricate channels trace this delicate necklace like the paths of a tidal garden. A settlement musician wore it while testing the quiet pipes that once carried warning notes through the reeds.

The greatest pearl ever found in the waters of Balar, given by Thingol to the Lord of Belegost as payment for the Dwarves' labour in delving Menegroth, the Thousand Caves. Its sheen is as starlight on the foam of the sea, and the Dwarves treasured it above all gems of their hoard. To hold it is to feel the peace of the shores of Balar before the wars came, when the Falathrim sang beneath the stars.
An immense pearl shines with the pale sheen of foam beneath the stars. Its recovery from a flooded intake became the proudest entry in a salvage crew's ledger.

A green jewel made by Enerdhil the smith in Gondolin, filled with the light of the Sun. Those who look through it see withered things as young once more, and the hands of one who wears it bring healing. Idril gave it to her son Eärendil, and through him it passed out of the Elder Days. It is called 'Elessar', the Elfstone, and great destiny lies upon it in ages yet to come.
A green jewel concentrates a warm, sunlike light. Through it, withered things appear young again, and the wearer's hands gain a healing touch.

The Nauglamir; a carcanet of gold set with a multitude of shining gems of Valinor, made by the Dwarves of Ered Luin for Finrod Felagund. It is the most renowned work of their craft in the Elder Days, and despite its weight of gold and jewels it lies upon the neck light as a strand of flax.
A multitude of bright gems hangs from finely joined gold links. Careful balancing makes the rich necklace lie as lightly as a strand of thread against the neck.

This ring was wrought by Mairon in the earliest darkness of the First Age, when he still moved among the Valar feigning faithfulness to the light. Drawn to Melkor's mastery, he fled in secret to Angband and there, in forges where no light had fallen since the world was young, he shaped this band as a token of his allegiance. Shadows and Unlight cling to it, and to wear it is to feel the cold cunning of the Enemy's chief servant.
Darkness clings to a band made for an officer of the engine's secret inspection bureau. Its cold precision recalls a system in which every helpful report might also be an accusation.

The crown of Daeron the Minstrel, loremaster of Doriath and inventor of the Cirth, the runes of Middle-earth. His songs were reckoned second only to those of the Ainur, though his love for Lúthien was unrequited. '...Daeron the Dark with ferny crown played with bewildering wizard's art music for breaking of the heart.'
Fern-like metalwork crowns the instrument keeper's brow. Its music belongs to a flooded conservatory where the last performances were recorded as maintenance reports.

The crown of Fëanor, greatest of the Noldor. It is beautifully wrought with many shining jewels of Valinor, whose light is a challenge to those born of darkness. Though his flaws ran deep, this crown is a reminder of his greatness, and of the terrible Oath that binds his sons to darkness. "Dear-bought those songs shall be accounted, and yet shall be well-bought.  For the price could be no other."
Bright jewels surround this crown with a radiance hostile to creatures of darkness. Its exceptional workmanship cannot hide the binding curse carried by the old furnace office.

The crown of Maedhros, High King of the Noldor, who was captured by Morgoth and hung by his right hand from Thangorodrim. The weight of the Oath of Fëanor rests heavily upon it, a curse that drives its wearer to doom even as it grants them kingly will. When worn with his hauberk, one feels the full measure of his endurance.
A command crown strengthens the wearer's will while imposing a binding curse. Wear it with its matching hauberk to gain the full benefit of their shared endurance enchantment.

The silver crown of Nargothrond, worn by Finrod Felagund, mightiest of the sons of Finarfin, who gave his life in defence of Beren at Tol-in-Gaurhoth. When Gorthaur challenged him to a contest of songs in that dreadful place, Finrod sang of the light of Valinor and the glory of the Elder Days, and for a time his music held the dark lord's power at bay. He cast aside this crown when he swore his oath to Beren and went forth into Angband disguised. It remembers his defiant song and stirs the same courage in its bearer.

A silver crown was worn by the speaker who coordinated the refuge shelters during the engine failure. It strengthens the courage needed to keep a clear voice when competing commands threaten to overwhelm it.

A deep green robe patterned with gold, once worn by Andreth the Wise, a mortal woman of Beor's House who debated with Finrod Felagund on the fate of Men and Elves. Though she loved Aegnor and was loved in return, they were sundered by the doom of their kinds. It sharpens the senses.
Gold patterns cross a deep green scholar's robe. The old survey college prepared it to sharpen the senses during delicate observations.

The White Lady of the Noldor once wore this robe, cut of the finest white cloth and hemmed with silver thread. Aredhel loved to ride and hunt in the wild lands, and though Eol ensnared her in Nan Elmoth, the robe remembers her freedom and quickens the wearer's step.
Fine white cloth is hemmed with silver thread. Made for a courier who travelled between distant tide stations, the robe quickens its wearer's step.

A robe that belonged to Idril Celebrindal, the golden-haired princess of Gondolin and only child of King Turgon. She alone foresaw the city's doom and prepared the secret way of escape that saved the survivors. Celebrindal means 'Silverfoot', for she went barefoot even in the snows. The soft folds invigorate the wearer and fill the heart with thoughts of the swift eagles of Manwë, who watched over the Hidden City from afar.
Soft folds carry an invigorating enchantment intended for emergency route inspectors. Wearing the robe encourages thoughts of open air above the machinery's confined passages.

This armour bears the weight of sorrow and treachery alike. It was worn by Gorlim, called the Unhappy, one of Barahir's outlaws in Dorthonion after the Dagor Bragollach had laid that land waste. When his beloved Eithel was taken from him, Gorthaur's servants promised her return if he would betray his lord. Driven beyond endurance, Gorlim revealed Barahir's hiding place - only to learn Eithel was already dead and the promise but a lie. He was slain, and this armour has been black with shame ever since.
Dark leather bears the marks of a disgraced inspector's office. Its old records contain falsified clearance certificates, and the armour still carries the oppressive stain of that work.

Leather armour worn by Haldad, chieftain of the Haladin and father of Haleth the Hunter. He fell defending his people when orcs besieged them in the stockade at the confluence of the Ascar and Gelion. Hardened by that desperate stand, it lends courage to those who must hold the line.
Worn leather was reinforced for defenders of an isolated flood barrier. It lends courage to anyone forced to hold a narrow line while others find safety.

Leather armour fashioned from the hide of some great hunting cat of the wild, perhaps one of the fell beasts that served Tevildo, Prince of Cats, in the days before Huan humbled him. Its proportions seem strange, yet it fits perfectly when donned. The wearer moves with feline grace and feels a predator's desire to hunt awakening within.
A great hunting cat's hide forms armour of unusual proportions that nevertheless fits when donned. It lends feline grace and awakens a predator's desire to hunt.

The armour of Beor the Old, father of the First House of the Edain and first of Men to meet the Elves. Finrod Felagund found him singing by a waterfall in Ossiriand and became his friend. Beor served Finrod until his death, and his house remained faithful ever after. Though worn and simple, this armour was lovingly cared for, and it gladdens the heart in the dark places of the world.
Simple old leather has been repaired with evident affection. Its steadying enchantment offers comfort in dark places, as it once did to a founder of the tide settlements.

Crafted for Aegnor, fourth son of Finarfin, who with his brother Angrod held the highlands of Dorthonion against Morgoth's hosts. He loved the mortal woman Andreth, yet refused to wed her lest war take him and leave her widowed. He fell in the fires of the Dagor Bragollach, and his love remained forever unfulfilled. This armour lends his fierce determination.
This armour was prepared for a storm-watch commander who refused to abandon an exposed station. It lends fierce determination to the wearer.

Armour wrought of Galvorn, a metal devised by Eol the Dark Elf in Nan Elmoth. Black and shining as jet, yet hard as Dwarf-steel, Galvorn could be beaten thin and supple and still turn any blade. Eol made this suit for his son Maeglin, who wore it when he came to Gondolin. It carries echoes of the shadows of Nan Elmoth and of the treachery that would one day doom the Hidden City.

Black, shining dusksteel has been beaten thin enough to remain supple without losing its strength. It came from a private engine workshop whose inspection marks were later found on sabotaged gate machinery.

A bright mail corslet worn by Fingon the Valiant, who alone dared climb Thangorodrim to rescue Maedhros from Morgoth's torment. When he could not loose the iron band, Thorondor bore him aloft and he cut off his friend's hand to free him. Fingon became High King after Fingolfin fell, and wore this gilded mail until the Nirnaeth Arnoediad. It shines like the sun and fills the wearer with the courage that defied Morgoth's shadow.
Gilded rings shine with a warm, sunlike brightness. This corslet was made for rescue crews, and its enchantment lends the courage to enter places others have already fled.

A corslet from the treasury of Durin the Deathless, eldest of the Seven Fathers of the Dwarves, who awoke beneath Mount Gundabad and founded Khazad-dum. He lived so long that he was called Deathless, and his folk believed his spirit would return in his heirs. This mail is wrought with the skill of the eldest days, proof against fire and frost, and it mends the hurts of battle as Durin's line endures through the ages.
An old workshop treasury preserved this finely joined corslet through generations of repairs. Its wards protect against fire and frost while helping battle wounds mend.

A suit of mail once worn by Maedhros, eldest son of Fëanor. Stripped from him when he was hung from Thangorodrim, it was stored in Morgoth's iron vaults. It is stained with the memory of torment and the unbreakable Oath that drives Fëanor's kin. When worn with his crown, one feels the full measure of his endurance.

A matching command hauberk was stored among the regent's confiscated equipment. A binding curse remains in its rings; worn with its companion crown, it grants the full measure of their endurance enchantment.

A heavy coat of mail from the hill of Amon Rudh, where the Petty-dwarves once dwelt in their hidden halls. Túrin Turambar sheltered there with his outlaws, until treachery brought ruin. The armour carries the stubbornness of that doomed hill, where defiance outlasted hope.
Heavy mail bears a hill shelter's stubborn protective craft. Its enchantment favours defiance when shelter and reinforcements have both failed.

The shining mail of Finwë, first High King of the Noldor, wrought in Valinor before the Darkening. When Morgoth came to Formenos with Ungoliant, Finwë alone stood against him and was slain—the first of the Eldar to die in Aman. The Dark Lord took this corslet along with the Silmarils. It still gleams with the light of the Blessed Realm, untouched by the Shadow that claimed its bearer.
Exceptionally bright mail was sealed in a storage chest before the engine catastrophe. Its surface still carries the clear radiance of a workshop that understood how to preserve light in metal.

The mail of Gundor, eldest son of Hador Goldenhead, who fell alongside his father at Eithel Sirion defending the rearguard of Fingolfin in the Dagor Bragollach. Though young, he slew many before he was overcome. This corslet grants strength to those who must stand against many foes.
A reinforced corslet was built for a barrier crew's youngest guard. Its enchantment grants strength when the wearer must stand against many opponents.

When Turgon departed Vinyamar in Nevrast, he left this armour, and strange destiny has led it far from those halls. It is crafted with a double layer of mail, which makes it too heavy for many, but turns blows that might cleave through a lesser suit.
Two layers of mail make this suit too heavy for many wearers. The burden buys protection against blows that could cleave a lighter harness.

This exquisite corslet was wrought in Gondolin by smiths who worked mithril brought from Valinor. Its rings are almost too small to see, yet each holds an echo of the stars Varda kindled before the awakening of the Elves. The Sindar called those stars 'the Swordsmen of the Sky', for they blazed forth to strike fear into Morgoth's heart. When darkness presses close, this mail gleams with their remembered light.
Almost invisible lumesilver rings catch and return pale points of light. The corslet gleams most clearly when darkness closes around it.

A black shield with scalloped edges, bearing the emblem of a white hand dripping blood. Such was the sign of certain orc-captains who swore blood-oaths to Morgoth, marking their hands in token of lives they would take. The shield grants fell strength to its bearer, but treachery clings to it, for those who bore this sign thought nothing of betraying their own.
A black, scallop-edged shield displays a white hand marked with red. The old enforcement emblem accompanies a strengthening enchantment and an abiding risk of treachery.

The shield of Glorfindel, Lord of the House of the Golden Flower in Gondolin. When the Hidden City fell, he led the survivors through the mountains and faced a Balrog in single combat upon a narrow ledge. He slew the demon but fell with it into the abyss. His sacrifice ensured Tuor and Idril's escape, and legend tells that he was re-embodied by the Valar for his valour.
A golden flower marks the shield of a mountain rescue company. Its battered rim records years spent holding narrow evacuation routes open for slower travellers.

A small iron shield inscribed with spiralling runes that wind inward to a central spike. Its name means 'Shield-curse' in Sindarin, for it was wrought by the loremasters of Doriath to turn aside the dark sorceries of Morgoth's servants. The runes are words of unbinding and freedom, and the spike was made to pierce enchanted armour. With this shield, one may break the chains that the Enemy lays upon the will.
Spiralling inscriptions lead inward to a spike on this small iron shield. Its wards resist hostile bindings, and the spike was prepared to pierce enchanted armour.

The famed shield of Hador Goldenhead, Lord of Dor-lomin and greatest chieftain of the Edain. His house was blessed by the Eldar, and the golden light of his hair passed to his descendants. This shield withstood the fires of Angband and the bitter cold of the North.
A veteran commander's shield bears the wear of furnace fires and frozen upland watches. Its wards protect against both fire and cold.

A shining blue shield set with crystals, borne by Fingolfin, High King of the Noldor, when he rode alone to challenge Morgoth before the gates of Angband. Seven times he wounded the Dark Lord with Ringil ere he fell, and Morgoth went ever after halt of one foot from those wounds.
Blue panels and bright crystals cover a shining shield. It was the ceremonial issue of a tide-gate marshal who insisted that equipment for public display must also survive field service.

This shield bears the device of the Blessed Realm, wrought in the light of the Two Trees before the Darkening. It shines like the full moon upon the sea, a memory of Valinor when all was unmarred. Those who bear it feel the peace of the Undying Lands, and their hearts are gladdened.
A bright shield carries the emblem of the settlements before their gates were divided by war. Its moonlike sheen calms and heartens the bearer.

A long tapering shield wrought of wood overlaid with plates of white metal, bearing the device of a swan's wing upon a field of deep blue. It was left in Turgon's abandoned halls of Vinyamar at the command of Ulmo, Lord of Waters, to await the messenger who would one day come to warn of Gondolin's doom. Tuor son of Huor found it upon the shore of Nevrast and bore it to the Hidden City. Untarnished by the long years of waiting, it lends its wearer endurance against the breaking of the heart.
White metal plates cover a long wooden shield decorated with a swan's wing against blue. It was kept at a coastal emergency station, and its enchantment helps the bearer endure heartbreak.

The hunting knife of Mablung of Doriath, captain of Thingol's guard. After Carcharoth was slain in the Hunting of the Wolf, Mablung cut the Silmaril from the beast's belly with this blade. Its edge is pitiless against wolves, and it lends the keen-eyed focus of its master.
A harbour warden's hunting knife has a keen, workmanlike point. Its edge is especially effective against wolves, and it sharpens the bearer's focus.

The dagger of Azaghal, Lord of Belegost, who stood against Glaurung the Father of Dragons in the Nirnaeth Arnoediad when all others fled. The Dwarves alone could withstand the dragon's gaze, and when Glaurung bore down upon Azaghal, the Dwarf-lord drove this blade into the dragon's belly—the first wound Glaurung ever suffered. Azaghal died crushed beneath the wyrm, but Glaurung fled in agony. The blade is still black with dragon-blood and burns with the wrath of Belegost.
Black dragon blood stains a dagger made for close defence against huge scaled creatures. Its enchantment carries the heat and fury of the furnace workshop that built it.

An Elf-wrought knife, finely balanced and keen. It was a birthday-gift that Húrin Thalion gave to his son Túrin, and Túrin bore it through many hard years. It lends steadiness of heart and a stubborn refusal to be ensnared or held.
A finely balanced knife was prepared as a personal gift by a travelling armourer. It steadies the heart and helps its bearer resist snares and binding.

'...the knife of the north, in Nogrod smithied.' A keen-edged dagger forged by the smiths of Nogrod in the Blue Mountains, whose craft was renowned across all Beleriand. Its edge never dulls, proof of the art that produced Angrist and the Dragon-helm alike, and its blade is perfectly balanced for throwing. The Dwarves made it for trade along the great roads with the Sindar, though none who bore it are remembered in the songs of those days.
A northern workshop dagger retains a keen edge despite long use. Its perfectly balanced blade is particularly suited to throwing.

A blade of black obsidian set in a hilt of twisted thorn-wood, perhaps fashioned by the Petty-dwarves in the years of their exile, or by some darker hand. The stone is slick with venom that never dries, and blood spilled upon it vanishes as though drunk by the wood itself. Those who bear it grow pale and hungry, yet find their footsteps grow ever lighter.

Black obsidian sits in a twisted thornwood hilt, its surface wet with enduring venom. The blade drinks spilled blood and brings pallor and hunger to its bearer, whose footsteps nevertheless grow lighter.

Forged from meteoric iron by Telchar of Nogrod, this dagger slices through iron as easily as flesh, earning its name: 'Iron Cleaver'. Curufin bore it until Beren wrested it from him. In Angband, while Morgoth slumbered under Lúthien's enchantment, Beren cut a Silmaril from the Iron Crown with this blade. When he reached for a second jewel, the knife snapped upon the crown and Morgoth stirred. Even broken, it remains peerless among daggers.

A meteoric-iron dagger was designed to cut stubborn metal fittings out of damaged machinery. Its edge parts iron as readily as flesh; even after breaking against a resistant mounting, it remains an exceptional blade.

A cruel curved blade of black iron, forged in the pits of Orodruth in the years when Morgoth's power was unchallenged and the Elves yet slumbered by Cuiviénen. It is famed among the orcs as a slayer of Elves and Men, and chieftains have fought and murdered for the right to bear it. Its edge drains the wielder's spirit even as it grants fell strength.
A cruel black curved blade became a contested badge among the regent's captains. It is particularly deadly to humans and elves, lending strength while draining the wielder's spirit.

A curved blade whose name means 'Blood-cutlass' in Sindarin, for its steel is stained the colour of old blood that no cleaning can remove. Some say it was forged by a Noldor smith driven mad by the Doom of Mandos, who quenched the blade in the blood of his own kin. It drinks deeply of those it wounds, sustaining its wielder even as it wakes a terrible hunger within them and clouds their mind with red thoughts.
Old red stains remain in the steel of this curved blade. It draws sustenance from its victims for the wielder, but brings a fierce hunger and clouds thought with violent urges.

A rune-etched knife of Mim, last of the Petty-dwarves who dwelt on Amon Rudh. His folk were the first Dwarves to enter Beleriand, exiled by their own kin, and they hated all others. When Túrin sheltered with him, Mim betrayed him to Morgoth's orcs for gold. The runes upon this blade exude venom, and a curse clings to it still—the bitterness of a diminished people and the treachery that brought their line to ruin.
