Etched channels carry venom along a short blade from an abandoned hillside workshop. A bitter curse remains in the inscriptions.

The hunting blade of Amrod, youngest son of Fëanor along with his twin Amras. In Valinor, the brothers hunted with Oromë and Celegorm beneath the light of the Trees. Of all Fëanor's sons, they were the least eager for the Oath, yet they followed their father into exile. This blade carries the skill of those hunts, sharpening the senses and silencing the hunter's step.
A hunter's blade was tuned for quiet patrols beyond the tide barriers. It sharpens the senses and muffles the wearer's step.

The 'dark-slayer'; a blade borne by Beren son of Barahir through the perils of Nan Dungortheb and into the pits of Angband itself. With this sword he fought beside the Hound of Valinor against the servants of Morgoth. It sheds a pale light that heartens the bearer in dark places.
A compact sword sheds a pale, heartening light. Its scabbard bears a route marker used by crews travelling through unlit service galleries.

This blade was taken up by Galadriel, daughter of Finarfin and mightiest of the Noldorin women, when Fëanor's host turned upon the Teleri at Alqualondë to seize their white ships. She fought fiercely against the Kinslayers in defence of her mother's kin, yet the Doom of Mandos fell upon her nonetheless when she crossed the sea in pride, seeking a realm of her own to rule. The blade remembers both her valour and her sorrow.
A finely made blade bears salt stains beneath its old polish. It was carried by harbour defenders during disputes over evacuation berths, and its craft retains both fierce resolve and sorrow.

A bright long-knife of Gondolin, forged in the days when that hidden city still stood in glory. Its cold light kindles at the nearness of orc-kind, and its keen point is a bane to great spiders and crawling terrors. Though little is spoken of this blade in the songs of Beleriand, strange fate is woven about it, and it will yet play a part in tales unwritten.
A bright long-knife kindles with cold light when orcs approach. Its keen point is particularly dangerous to great spiders and other crawling horrors.

A slender, gilded sword once wielded by Idril Celebrindal, Princess of Gondolin. She alone foresaw the city's doom and prepared the secret way of escape. The blade gleams with golden light, lending courage and grace to its bearer, and no snare or enchantment can easily hold them.
A slender gilded sword carries a warm golden radiance. It lends courage and grace while helping its bearer remain free of snares and hostile binding.

The hunting blade of Amras, twin brother of Amrod. Like his brother, he  rejoiced in the hunt, riding often with Celegorm in the woods of  Valinor. Though bound by the terrible Oath, he dwelt long in the wild  lands of East Beleriand, far from the wars of Angband. This blade grants  the mastery of two weapons, striking with the swift accord of the twins.
A hunting sword was made for paired-weapon training at the refuge watch school. It grants mastery of two blades moving in swift accord.

A sword forged in the secret forges of Gondolin, gleaming like a blade of winter ice when drawn. The Orcs knew it as the Goblin-cleaver and fled before its edge, for it was wrought to be their especial bane. It is the mate to Glamdring, the Foe-hammer, and when both blades are wielded together they sing in sharp accord, as they did in the Elder Days when the lords of Gondolin bore them against the hosts of Morgoth.
Breachfang shines cold and bright, and was made especially deadly to orcs. Wield it with its companion Gateknell to awaken their shared enchantment.

The 'Foe-hammer', forged by Enerdhil of Gondolin and borne by Turgon, King of the Hidden City. Its edge is the bane of orcs, trolls, dragons, and Balrogs alike. It is the mate to Orcrist, the Goblin-cleaver, and when both blades are wielded together, they sing in harmony as they did in the Elder Days.
Gateknell was prepared for defenders facing orcs, trolls, dragons, and demons. Its companion Breachfang brings out their full power when both swords are wielded together.

Forged by Telchar of Nogrod, greatest of the Dwarf-smiths, this blade is called the sword of Sun and Moon, for Nar is the flame and Sil the silver light, and between them it burns with both. Its edge has known the blood of darkness and the warmth of starlight alike, wrought in the deep fires of the Blue Mountains with all of Telchar's art. Yet a greater fate is written upon it than any tale of the Elder Days may tell.
A master workshop bound both flame and pale radiance into this blade. The contrasting lights follow its edge as it turns in the hand.

The sword of Elu Thingol, High King of the Sindar, whose name means 'King's Ire' in the tongue of his people. For three ages of starlight Thingol ruled in Doriath, and this blade was with him when he led the Sindar against Morgoth's orcs. Its jeweled hilt fills the bearer with the pride and will of that ancient king, though such confidence may draw peril as surely as it wards off fear.
Bright stones decorate a commander's sword-hilt. The enchantment grants proud resolve, but the same confidence can draw danger to its bearer.

The black sword Anglachel, forged by Eol of Nan Elmoth from star-iron. It was brought to Thingol in Doriath, and later borne by Beleg Cuthalion. Its edge is dreadful keen, and a cold will seems to wake when it is drawn. Many have found that mischance follows where this blade passes—as though it remembers every death it has dealt.
Cold purpose seems to stir in this black star-iron blade when it is drawn. Its dreadful edge is accompanied by persistent mischance.

The sable sword reforged from Anglachel, wielded by Túrin. Its blade can slice iron like parchment, and it drinks deeply of blood. A fell curse  lies upon it: once unsheathed, it must taste blood. The sword's grim will  fills its master with fearless despair, drawing mighty foes nigh—and  giving strength to slay them.

A reforged black sword slices through iron and drinks blood. Once drawn, its curse demands blood, while its grim influence banishes fear, draws powerful enemies near, and gives strength to fight them.

The sister-blade to Anglachel, forged by Eol the Dark Elf in Nan Elmoth from the iron heart of a fallen star. Eol kept Anguirel for himself while giving Anglachel to Thingol as payment for dwelling in his realm. When Eol pursued his fleeing wife and son to Gondolin, his son Maeglin stole this sword and bore it ever after. A bitter blade by brooding Eol forged, in secret made of metal from a star.
A bitterly finished sword was forged from the heart of a fallen star. Its maker kept this companion to another black blade in a private workshop, away from the public armoury records.

A sword forged in Vinyamar during Turgon's dwelling in Nevrast, before he departed to build Gondolin. Its name means 'Blue-sword' in Sindarin, for its blade has the grey-blue colour of the sea beneath clouds, and its hilt is white as foam. The cold winds of Nevrast are bound within it, warding off frost and holding the bearer free from snaring spells. It strikes swift and true as the sea-birds of that coast.
A grey-blue blade and white hilt resemble a cloudy sea and its foam. The sword resists frost and binding magic, moving with a swift, true stroke.

The blade of Nan, a giant who dwelt in the frozen wastes north of Angband in the years before the rising of the Sun. Such creatures served Morgoth in those dark times, though they were few and wild. This sword is massive beyond mortal scale, yet one of great strength may wield it. When swung, it cleaves through armour and bone alike, impaling foes upon its length.
An immense sword was made for a fighter far stronger than an ordinary person. Its long blade cleaves armour and bone and can impale foes along its length.

A greatsword borne by Saithnar, an Elf-lord of the host of Fingolfin who fell fighting the houseless spirits and revenants that Morgoth sent forth from Angband. Its silver runes blaze against the undead, but the spirits of those Saithnar slew cling to the blade still, haunting its wielder with visions of ancient battles and the faces of the restless dead.
Silver inscriptions flare when this greatsword meets the undead. Spirits cling to the blade, burdening its wielder with visions of old battles and restless faces.

A cruel and heavy blade, wreathed in undying flames that burn without consuming. It was forged in the deepest pits of Angband for Gothmog, Lord of Balrogs and High Captain of Morgoth's hosts. With this sword he enforced the Dark Lord's will among the orc-hosts, and none dared defy him. The flames that wreathe it are of the same fire that burns within the Valaraukar themselves, cold-killing and terrible to behold.
Undying flames surround a cruel, heavy sword without consuming it. A furnace captain used the weapon to enforce obedience, and its fire remains hostile to cold.

A legendary blade of mithril, sung of in the ancient lays of Valinor. Its curved edge crackles with lightning, and in battle it moves swift as the storm-wind. Few have wielded it since the Noldor came to Middle-earth, for such a weapon demands a hand of great skill. '...the sweeping sickle of the slashing tempest, the lambent lightning's leaping falchion, even Celeg Aithorn that shall cleave the world.'
Lightning crackles along the curved edge of a lumesilver blade. It moves with stormlike speed in battle and demands a skilled hand to govern it.

The weapon of Fingolfin, High King of the Noldor, who rode alone to Angband and challenged Morgoth to single combat. Seven times Ringil bit deep into the Dark Lord's flesh. Even as Morgoth crushed him, Fingolfin's last stroke hewed the foot of the Enemy, and Morgoth went halt ever after. The blade shines like a column of ice lit by light unquenchable, and its bitter cold burns the servants of darkness.
Cold light rises along the sword like an illuminated column of ice. Its bitter chill burns creatures of darkness.

A long blade that glows with pale light, its hilt wrapped in red leather. When Ungoliant fled from Morgoth's Balrogs, she spawned many foul children in the Ered Gorgoroth, and their webs filled the dread valley of Nan Dungortheb. The Noldor forged this sword to cleanse those mountains, and many of her spawn fell to its edge. It wards against venom and darkness, a bane to all who crawled forth from that lightless brood.
A red leather grip supports a long blade that glows with pale light. Prepared for clearing infested service galleries, it resists venom and darkness and is especially deadly to spiders.

The gleaming spear of Ingwe, High King of the Vanyar. Forged of mithril in Valinor, it is light as a feather yet stronger than steel. Though Ingwe sits forever at the feet of Manwë, this spear was borne by his son Ingwion in the War of Wrath, where it pierced the hearts of balrogs and cast down the dark towers of Thangorodrim.
A bright lumesilver spear is exceptionally light yet stronger than steel. It was carried by the crews assigned to destroy the cinder fiends guarding damaged engine towers.

The poisoned javelin of Eol the Dark Elf, forged in the shadows of Nan Elmoth. When Eol pursued Aredhel and Maeglin to Gondolin and Turgon denied him freedom, he hurled this spear at his son. Aredhel stepped before the blow, and none knew the point was poisoned until she died that night. For this murder Eol was cast from Caragdur.
A slender javelin conceals venom on its point. The old workshop report identifies the poison only in a later marginal warning, added after a fatal handling error.

A cruel spear, black-hafted with a head of dark bronze, forged by Gorthaur in the years after the Dagor Bragollach when he walked openly through Beleriand spreading despair among Men. Sauron poured much of his own malice into its making, for he was a Maia in his own right, and the weapon bites through flesh and spirit alike without distinction. It throws no shadow, for darkness was bound into it at its forging.
A black shaft carries a head of dark bronze. The spear wounds flesh and spirit alike, and casts no shadow because darkness was bound into its making.

The iron spear of Boldog, a name borne by the mightiest orc-captains of Angband. Some say 'Boldog' was a title given to fell spirits who took orc-shape to lead Morgoth's hosts. This one led raids against the marches of Doriath, hunting for Lúthien at his master's command. The spear is heavy and brutal, forged in the dark pits, and wolves flee before it remembering their dread captain's wrath.
A heavy iron spear served as an officer's badge in the regent's raiding companies. Wolves recoil from its threatening presence.

The spear of Gil-galad, last High King of the Noldor in Middle-earth, whose name means 'Snow-point' for its blade gleams white and is cold as ice to the touch. Gil-galad was young when Gondolin fell, but he grew to lead the remnants of his people at the Havens of Sirion. None could withstand Aeglos, and the servants of the Enemy fled before it, for its chill brings death to the undead and all fell spirits.
A white spearhead is cold as ice against the hand. Its chill is especially deadly to undead and hostile spirits.

A pack of three perfectly balanced throwing spears, crafted in the secret forges of Gondolin. They bear the emblem of a swallow in flight, the sigil of the House of the Swallow, whose lord Duilin was the swiftest of all the Eldalie to run and leap. Known as 'Tuilindor' in the High Elven tongue, these weapons fly true as the birds they are named for. They sing of the valiant defense of the northern walls, where the Swallow-folk rained death upon the encroaching dark.
Three throwing spears are perfectly matched and balanced for flight. A small bird emblem identifies the mobile watch unit that commissioned them.

A great spear with a point like a sharp thorn of steel, originally forged by the Noldor for hunting the great spiders of Nan Dungortheb. Ogbar, a chieftain of the Easterlings who served Morgoth, slew its bearer in the treachery of the Nirnaeth Arnoediad and claimed it as spoil. Though made for nobler hands, the spear's virtue remains—its edge is death to the spawn of Ungoliant, and it pierces the thickest spider-hide with ease.
A great spear ends in a narrow steel thorn. Its original spider-hunting enchantment survives the loss of its first owner and still penetrates thick spider hide with ease.

The black spear of Melkor Morgoth, mightiest of the Ainur who fell, wielded in the hour when he and the great spider Ungoliant came in darkness to the heart of Valinor. With this weapon he struck the Two Trees of Yavanna - Telperion the White and Laurelin the Gold—and Ungoliant's venom poured into the wounds until all the light of the world was swallowed. The weapon still carries a sliver of that primal malice, and even to touch it is to feel the cold of the Unlight that once shrouded the land in darkness.
A black spear was used to rupture the weather engine's living power conduits. A trace of that destructive darkness remains in the metal, making even a touch feel unnaturally cold.

A sharp and well-made axe gifted to Haldan, Lord of the Men of Brethil, by the Dwarves of the Blue Mountains. When he asked its name, the Dwarves replied 'Binahkram'—meaning 'without name' in their secret tongue, for they do not share true names with outsiders. The Haladin, not understanding, took this as the axe's name, and so it has been called ever since. It bites deep into orc-flesh and spider-hide alike.
A sharp, well-made axe bears a workshop inventory mark where a ceremonial name might usually be engraved. Its edge is particularly effective against orcs and spiders.

The axe of Durin the Deathless, eldest of the Seven Fathers of the Dwarves, who awoke alone beneath Mount Gundabad and founded Khazad-dum. Its haft is carved with the symbols of all Seven Fathers. A sapphire in the blade glows softly in darkness, for Durin first beheld his reflection in the Mirrormere and saw a crown of stars above his head. The axe feels light in hand and bolsters the hearts of those who delve deep.
Workshop emblems cover an axe-haft beneath a softly glowing sapphire. The axe feels light in the hand and bolsters the courage of those who descend into deep passages.

The great axe of Tuor, son of Huor, wrought for him by the smiths of Gondolin. Its name is 'Thudder-sharp' for it strikes with the force of a club but cuts like a sword. Tuor wielded it in the Fall of Gondolin, where he slew Maeglin and cast him from the walls, and clove through countless orcs and trolls defending Idril and his son Eärendil.
A great axe combines a club's force with a sword's keen cut. It was prepared for rescuers breaking through orcs and trolls along an evacuation route.

A dark axe with a wicked and hungry edge, forged in the deepest pits of Angband by Morgoth Bauglir himself for the breaking of kin and the severing of hope. Many are the lives it has claimed, and each one it remembers: it is blood-warm to the touch and thirsting always for vitality, drinking deeply of those it wounds. Those who wield it are haunted by the cries of the slain—mothers weeping over fallen sons in the wars of Beleriand.
A dark axe stays blood-warm and draws vitality from those it wounds. Its wielder is haunted by the cries left behind after its killings.

Forged beneath Mount Dolmed by Gamil Zirak, master of Telchar and greatest smith of Nogrod in his time. The Dwarven road from Nogrod to Belegost ran through that mountain's pass, and this axe guarded it against Morgoth's servants for many years. It is an heirloom of Nogrod, granting strength to lift its great weight and fire in the blood to face the Balrogs and their kin.
A mountain-pass workshop forged this weighty axe for road guards. It grants strength enough to lift its mass and fierce courage against cinder fiends and their kin.

A great axe forged in Belegost, the northern Dwarven city of the Blue Mountains. Both blade and haft are made from a single piece of blackened steel. Engraved upon the axehead are the names of Belegost's valiant fallen—warriors who stood against Morgoth's trolls when they descended from Angband. It is called 'Mazarbulbark' in the Dwarven tongue, meaning 'the axe that is written upon', and it fills its wielder with vengeance.
Blade and haft form a single piece of blackened steel. Engraved names record guards killed by trolls, and the great axe carries their surviving company's desire for vengeance.

The immense, blackened steel axe of Gothmog, Lord of Balrogs and High Captain of Angband. Flames crawl along its edge, and it strikes with such force that it can hew down many foes in a single sweep. The weapon burns with an evil will, rousing wrath and noise, loath to be put aside.
Flames crawl along the edge of an immense blackened axe. It can strike several foes in one sweep, but its hostile will encourages wrath and noise and resists being put aside.

A sleek hand axe forged by Maeglin, Lord of the House of the Mole, who learned his father Eol's secrets of working Galvorn and star-iron. The blade is dark as a moonless night and cuts through armour with ease. Maeglin delved deep beneath Gondolin seeking metals and gems, and his skill was great—yet he betrayed the Hidden City to Morgoth for the promise of Idril. This axe remembers that treachery in its very edge.
A sleek dark hand axe carries a deep-delver's exceptional metalwork. It cuts through armour readily, though treachery remains in its enchantment.

A massive glaive forged by the Dwarves of the Blue Mountains in the years before the rising of the Sun, when Morgoth's creatures first assailed their halls. Gaurin was a champion of those ancient Dwarves, and with this blade he broke through the walls of Rodrim's hall when orcs had sealed the gates. Its edge cleaves stone and steel alike, and it may yet be enchanted further by a skilled smith. '...the glaive of Gaurin whose gleaming stroke did rive the rocks of Rodrim's hall.'
A massive glaive was made to breach rock and steel where sealed gates trapped a work crew. Its powerful edge can still accept further enchantment from a skilled smith.

Named for the great River Sirion that flowed through the heart of Beleriand, this glaive moves like its waters—ever restless, seeking every gap and opening. The Sirion was the mightiest river of those lands, and many realms rose and fell along its banks. In battle, this blade flows around defences and strikes where foes least expect.
This glaive was shaped for defenders fighting along narrow water channels. Its flowing movement seeks gaps in a foe's guard and strikes around defences.

A glaive of mithril upon a shaft of dark Nan Elmoth wood, forged by the Noldor in their early years in Beleriand. 'Silver-cleaver' it is named in Sindarin, for its edge parts armour as easily as cloth. The blade feels alive and eager, granting unnatural speed and precision, but the fey spirit bound within it feeds on the wielder's strength.
A lumesilver glaive rests on a dark wooden shaft. Its edge parts armour readily and grants unnatural speed and precision, but the spirit within feeds on its wielder's strength.

The staff of Halmir, chieftain of the Haladin who dwelt in the Forest of Brethil. When the hosts of Morgoth marched south in the Nirnaeth Arnoediad, Halmir gathered his people and led them to war, though he was old. He died ere the battle, but his son Haldir fought in his stead, and the Haladin held their ground when all else fled. This staff embodies his steadfast will against the Shadow.
An old settlement leader's staff was preserved by the watch company that followed its bearer. Its enchantment strengthens steadfast resolve against darkness.

The staff of doom borne by Turgon, King of Gondolin, when he sat upon his high throne to pronounce judgment. None could gainsay his decrees, for he was stern and proud as his father Fingolfin. With this staff he declared the fates of all who came before him, and even condemned Eol to death for the slaying of Aredhel. Its bearer commands the same dread majesty as the Hidden King who defied Morgoth until the very end.
A judgement staff marked the authority of the chief gate adjudicator. It grants its bearer a commanding, dreadful majesty.

The great hammer of Telchar of Nogrod, mightiest of all Dwarven smiths. With this hammer he forged Angrist the iron-cleaver, Narsil the sword of kings, and the Dragon-helm of Dor-lomin. Its hard steel has rung upon forge and anvil in the making of legendary works, yet it served equally well upon orc-shields when Morgoth's hosts descended upon the halls of the Dwarves.
Hard steel carries the wear of both anvil work and military service. This master smith's hammer was equally at home shaping fine equipment and breaking an attacker's shield.

A hammer wrought by Aulë himself in the days following the destruction of the Two Trees, and carried from Valinor by mighty Rog, Lord of the House of the Hammer of Wrath. It has a haft and head of black iron banded about with red gold and strikes with earth-shattering force, sundering armour and bone alike.
Red gold bands a hammer's black iron head and haft. Its tremendous impact shatters armour and bone with the force of a collapsing foundation.

A mighty Dwarven mattock forged by Gamil Zirak, master smith of Nogrod and teacher of Telchar. Its name in Khuzdul means 'Axe-lord', for it was made for a king of Nogrod in the early days. Enchanted for both battle and mine, its heavy head crushes rock and skull with equal ease, and it can hew through stone as though it were rotten wood. Many are the tunnels delved by this tool, and many the foes it has broken.
A mighty mattock was commissioned for a deep excavation master. Enchanted for mine and battle alike, its heavy head crushes skulls and cuts through stone with remarkable ease.

The helm of Angrod, third son of Finarfin and brother of Finrod, Aegnor, and Galadriel. With Aegnor he held the highlands of Dorthonion against Morgoth's hosts for centuries, until both brothers fell in the fires of the Dagor Bragollach. This helm remembers the bitter winds of those high places and the courage needed to face the terror of Morgoth's flames.
A weathered helm came from the exposed stations above the storm line. It preserves a cold-weather watch's endurance and the courage to face terrifying flame.

A helm worn by Curufin, fifth son of Fëanor and most like his father in skill of hand and cunning of mind. He was a master smith, yet his scheming brought ruin to Finrod's realm. The helm sharpens the wearer's craft and guile, but its treacherous whispers can never be silenced.
A workshop director's helm sharpens craft and guile. Treacherous whispers accompany its help and cannot be silenced.

A helm wrought of grey metal and set with the bones of an orc who dared raise his blade against his own master. In Angband, such treachery was punished with torments beyond imagining, yet this one's defiance was preserved in mockery. The helm carries the stain of betrayal, but also the power to break bonds—even the dread Oath of Fëanor holds less sway over one who wears it.
Grey metal surrounds bone taken from a soldier condemned for defying his commander. The helm retains a stain of betrayal, yet weakens imposed bonds, including the Furnace Covenant.

The Dragon-helm of Dor-lomin, forged by Telchar of Nogrod for Azaghal and given to Maedhros, who bestowed it upon Fingon. It passed to the House of Hador, and Túrin wore it when he was called the Dragon-helm. The servants of Morgoth fled before its terrible visage, for they deemed the spirit of the great worm Glaurung looked out from its eyes.
A dragon-shaped crest gives this helm a terrible face. Creatures serving the regent recoil from its gaze as though they faced a living monster.

A great black helm wrought in Utumno, Morgoth's first fortress beneath the mountains of the uttermost North. For uncounted ages Utumno festered in darkness while Morgoth bred his terrible servants. When the Valar broke its gates, many treasures were lost in the ruin. This helm survived, bearing still the malice of those lightless depths. It grants strength and will, yet bends the wearer's purpose toward its first dark master.
A great black helm survived the collapse of Karth's earliest buried works. It grants strength and will while bending the wearer's purpose toward the authority it originally served.

A great helm of Dwarvish make, wrought deep in Khazad-dum with curving horns of black iron and a face-guard hammered into a stern and defiant visage. The Dwarves of Durin's folk crafted such masks in the deeps, for they were pride-stiff even when the darkness pressed close. When the hosts of Angband marched south, the Dwarves donned such helms and none fled.
Curving black horns rise over a stern faceguard. This deep-forge helm was made for guards who needed to remain defiant when darkness closed around their position.

A mithril helm rising to a tall spike, worn by Ecthelion, Lord of the Fountains of Gondolin. When the city fell, he faced Gothmog, Lord of Balrogs, and drove the spike into the demon's breast as they plunged together into the Fountain of the King. Both perished, but the helm still echoes with the music of falling water.
A tall spike rises from a pale lumesilver helm. Its enchantment retains a soft echo like water falling through the engine's cooling courts.

The helm left by Turgon in his abandoned halls of Vinyamar, at the command of Ulmo Lord of Waters, for the messenger who would one day come to warn of Gondolin's doom. Tuor son of Huor found it there, crowned with three swan's feathers, and wore it when he came at last to the Hidden City. It greatens the heart and clarifies the purpose of the one who wears it, for it was touched by the will of Ulmo himself.
Three pale feathers crown a helm kept in a coastal emergency station. Its influence strengthens the heart and clarifies the wearer's purpose.

'His sword of steel was valiant.' A keen-edged longsword from the Havens of Sirion, whose name means 'Foam-cleaver' in the tongue of the Sindar. When Eärendil armed himself for the great voyage, this was the blade girded at his side. It sheds a faint light and grows eager in the hand when the shadow of dragons falls near, as though it remembers the ruin of Ancalagon the Black above the towers of Thangorodrim.
A keen steel longsword sheds faint light. It responds eagerly to nearby dragons, as befitted the patrol that guarded the ruined upper intakes.

'His shining shield was scored with runes to ward all wounds and harm from him.' A shield of mithril, the true silver, its face bright as starlight and inscribed with runes of warding by the loremasters of the Havens of Sirion. The mithril was brought from Khazad-dum, traded westward by the Dwarves through Ered Luin. Its name means 'Warding Shield' in Sindarin. The runes are words of staying and protection drawn from the deep lore the Noldor brought out of the West. Eärendil bore it when he sailed in Vingilot to plead before the Valar.
Protective inscriptions cover the bright surface of a lumesilver shield. Each line is part of a patient ward against wounds and harm.

'Of silver was his habergeon.' A corslet of mithril chain, the true silver of the Eldar, light and supple as water yet proof against any edge. Its rings shine like stars upon the sea, and the Eldar of Avernien named it 'Gilceleb', Star-silver. It was part of the panoply of ancient kings that Eärendil donned when he armed himself for his great voyage, bearing the craft of both Gondolin and Doriath in its making.
Tiny lumesilver rings make a corslet supple as flowing water. Its bright, close-woven links offer strong protection without a rigid shell.

'Of adamant his helmet tall, an eagle-plume upon his crest.' A great helm wrought of adamant, so hard that no blade could mar its surface. Upon its crest rises a plume fashioned in the likeness of an eagle's wing, in honour of Thorondor, King of Eagles, who aided the Noldor and the Edain against Morgoth. When Eärendil wore it upon the deck of Vingilot, the servants of the Enemy quailed before its terrible visage.
A tall adamant helm bears a plume shaped like a bird's wing. Its exceptionally hard surface and imposing crest make a threatening sight to hostile troops.

'His arrows shorn of ebony.' Arrows fashioned from the heartwood of ebony, black and heavy, shorn to a keen edge and fletched with dark feathers. The Eldar of the Havens called them 'Mornpilin', the Dark Arrows. They were crafted for the dragon-horn bow and fly far and true against the winged terrors of Morgoth. In the War of Wrath, such shafts brought ruin upon the dragon-host above Beleriand.
Dark feathers balance heavy shafts of ebony heartwood. Crafted for a dragon-horn bow, they are especially deadly to dragons.

A cloak worn by Maglor, second son of Fëanor and mightiest singer of the Noldor. Though bound by the Oath, he was the gentlest of his brothers and fostered Elrond and Elros after the sack of Sirion. When at last he held a Silmaril, it burned his hand, and he cast it into the sea. He wanders the shores still, and his songs of sorrow echo in this garment.
A singer's cloak retains the sorrowful resonance of performances given along abandoned shores. Its wearer hears something of those long, unfinished songs in the cloth.

The grey cloak of Elu Thingol, tallest of all the Eldar and King of Doriath, who ruled beneath the enchantments of his queen Melian in the hidden realm of Menegroth. Before even the Sun rose, Thingol heard the music of Ulmo by the waters of Cuiviénen and was moved to a wonder none could match. How this cloak passed from Doriath into the wider world, none can say. It bears the silver-grey of the beech forests beneath the Girdle, and its folds ward against flame and frost alike.
A silver-grey cloak was preserved in a settlement's forest shelter. Its folds protect against both flame and frost.

A shadowy cloak bestowed by Ulmo, Lord of Waters, upon Tuor at Vinyamar's shore when the Vala rose from the sea in storm and majesty. Ulmo alone among the Valar still watched over the exiled Elves and the Edain, and he sent Tuor to warn Turgon of Gondolin's doom. This cloak flows like deep currents, hiding the wearer from searching eyes and warding against the cold of deep places.
A dark cloak moves like a deep current around its wearer. It conceals the body from searching eyes and protects against cold.

A shadowy cloak woven by Lúthien Tinúviel from her own dark hair, which grew past her heels. With this garment and her enchanting song she cast Morgoth himself into slumber in the depths of Angband. Its folds deepen the shadows around the wearer and lull the watchful into sleep.
Dense shadow gathers in this dark woven cloak. Its folds deepen concealment and lull watchful creatures toward sleep.

The fell hide of Draugluin, sire and lord of all the werewolves of Morgoth, slain by Huan the Hound of Valinor at Tol-in-Gaurhoth. He was the mightiest wolf that ever walked, yet even he fell before Huan and crept dying to his master's feet. Beren wore this hide to pass the gates of Angband, and its dread shape may still deceive the Enemy.
The cured hide of a colossal wolf keeps the shape of a feared pack leader. As a disguise it may deceive the regent's servants into accepting the wearer.

The winged cloak of Thuringwethil, the vampire-messenger of Sauron who flew between Angband and Tol-in-Gaurhoth. Lúthien wore this fell garment to enter the throne room of Morgoth himself. Its great black wings still hold dark power, and servants of the Enemy may mistake its wearer for kin.
Great black wings fold into a mantle taken from a night messenger. Its dark enchantment may cause the regent's servants to mistake the wearer for one of their own.

The bow of Celegorm the Fair, third son of Fëanor, who in the days of Valinor hunted with Oromë the Great. The Vala gifted him Huan, the Hound of Valinor. But the Oath drove Celegorm to terrible deeds, and the bow clings to its bearer as the curse clung to him.
A hunter's bow carries a stubborn binding curse. Once taken up, it clings to its bearer.

A shortbow crafted in Doriath by the hunters who served under Beleg Cuthalion, the greatest archer of the Sindar. Though unadorned, its wood was cut from the heart of a yew that grew within the Girdle of Melian, where the Queen's power quickened all living things. When drawn, the archer's eye is guided as if by the foresight of the Maia herself, finding the gaps in armour and the weakness in every defence. The hunters called it 'Death's Sting' for the way its arrows found their mark unerringly.
An unadorned yew shortbow was grown from carefully tended stock in a sheltered tide garden. Its guiding enchantment finds gaps in armour and weak points in an enemy's defence.

The great bow of Beleg Cuthalion, mightiest archer among all the Children of Ilúvatar. Made of black yew and strung with Beleg's own hair, which shimmers a pale gold. With this bow he guarded the marches of Doriath, until treachery and darkness brought his doom at his friend's own hand. When paired with Dailir, the bow's power awakens fully.
Black yew limbs are strung with shimmering pale-gold hair. This bow's full power awakens when it shoots its matched arrow, Trueflight.

A longbow of Sindarin craft, its name meaning 'Bent-wood' in that tongue. The Sindar of Doriath were great hunters and archers, and this bow was made by their bowyers for the wardens of the marches. Though worn at the notches from years of faithful service, it remains supple and true. Its arrows fly straight and swift, unhindered by enchantment or shadow.
Years of service have worn the notches of a supple wooden longbow. Its arrows fly straight and swift through enchantment and shadow.

A tall longbow painted in many bright hues, crafted by the House of the Heavenly Arch whose lord was Egalmoth. His folk loved colour and light, and their gear shone with gems and bright enamels. When Gondolin fell, Egalmoth led the rearguard through the Cristhorn with Glorfindel, and many orcs fell to their bows. This weapon draws smooth and true, the aim steady, and each shot flies where a deft will sends it.
Bright colours cover a tall longbow made by an aqueduct watch workshop. It draws smoothly and rewards steady, deliberate aim.

'His bow was made of dragon-horn.' A great bow fashioned from the horn of a slain dragon in the Havens of Sirion, where the remnants of Gondolin and Doriath gathered after those realms fell. Its name means 'Dragon-cleaver' in the tongue of the Sindar. The Eldar of Avernien blessed it with many enchantments against the terrors of the Enemy, and it wards the mind against fear and confusion, a last gift of a dying age.
A great dragon-horn bow was assembled by the survivors of several ruined tide stations. Its wards protect the mind against fear and confusion.

The unerring arrow of Beleg Cuthalion, greatest archer of the Sindar. 'Dailir' means 'the Returner', for this arrow would always be found again after it was shot, no matter how far it flew. Beleg treasured it above all his arrows. When loosed from Belthronding, its power is greatest.
A treasured arrow can always be recovered after it is shot, regardless of how far it travels. Its greatest power is released when loosed from its companion bow, Reedbow.

Boots that belonged to Finrod Felagund, King of Nargothrond and friend of Men, who gave his life defending Beren in the pits of Tol-in-Gaurhoth. Even in chains he fought a werewolf with his bare hands and slew it, though the battle cost him his life. These boots were made for riding in Valinor, but they grant their wearer nimbleness on any ground, letting them pass through battle as a dance and slip free of any binding.
Riding boots from a refuge workshop lend nimbleness on any ground. Their enchantment supports evasive movement through battle and escape from binding.

These boots have been worn by more than one fugitive through the dread forest of Taur-nu-Fuin, where Morgoth's curse turned the fair woods of Dorthonion into a waste of shadow and malice, and the trees were bent to watch and betray. Beren passed through there on his long road to Nargothrond, driven near to madness by the whispers of the corrupted wood. These boots tread lightly upon rotting leaves, making no sound, and still carry some charm against the forest's spite.
Quiet boots have carried successive fugitives through a blighted forest. They tread silently over fallen leaves and retain a protective charm against the hostile place.

Boots bearing the insignia of the House of the Mole, whose lord was Maeglin, son of Eol and Aredhel. He delved deep beneath Gondolin seeking metals and gems, and his miners discovered the foundations of the city. Yet Maeglin's heart was dark, and his love for Idril twisted into the betrayal that doomed the Hidden City. These boots are covered in dark moleskin, and their wearer moves silent as shadow through the deep.
Dark moleskin covers a miner's boots. Their soft construction keeps the wearer's movements quiet in deep passages.

Greaves forged for Orodreth, who became King of Nargothrond after Finrod Felagund perished in Tol-in-Gaurhoth. Túrin's counsel led his realm to ruin, and Orodreth fell in the Battle of Tumhalad when Glaurung came against his host. These greaves were made to ward against dragonfire, though they could not save their bearer from the doom that the Father of Dragons brought upon the Hidden Kingdom of the Narog.
Heavy greaves were forged for a commander stationed near the damaged hot-air intakes. Their wards protect against dragonfire.

Greaves forged by the host of Fingolfin during the dreadful crossing of the Helcaraxe, the Grinding Ice between Araman and Middle-earth. When Fëanor burned the ships at Losgar and abandoned them, Fingolfin's people walked the ice rather than return in shame. Many perished in that crossing, but those who survived became hardened beyond breaking. These greaves carry the endurance of that terrible journey.
Greaves from a winter evacuation preserve the endurance of crews who crossed the frozen tidal flats on foot. Their lasting enchantment helps the wearer bear hardship.

Heavy greaves forged for Caranthir the Dark in Thargelion, the harshest and most quick-tempered of Fëanor's sons. His face burned red with fury at the Mereth Aderthad when he nearly came to blows with the sons of Finarfin, and his wrath only grew through the long wars. These iron-shod greaves are made for charging headlong into the enemy, and they carry something of his furious heat.
Iron-shod greaves favour a headlong charge. A furious heat accompanies their heavy onset.

These gloves bear the insignia of the House of the Swallow, whose lord Duilin was the swiftest of all the Eldar. His folk were famed as the greatest archers of Gondolin, raining death upon Morgoth's hosts from the northern walls. Duilin fell in their defence, struck by dragonfire even as he loosed arrow after arrow into the foe. These gloves steady the archer's hands and guide each shaft to its mark.
A flying-bird insignia marks gloves made for the northern wall archers. They steady the hands and guide each shaft toward its mark.

Gloves worn by Celebrimbor, son of Curufin and grandson of Fëanor, who inherited his forefather's skill at the forge yet rejected the Oath that cursed his house. In Nargothrond he crafted wonders of silver and gem, and he alone of his kin fought for Finrod against his own father and uncle. His greatest works still lie in the future, but these gloves grant steady hands for the finest craft.
A master workshop's gloves preserve a precise, steady touch. They lend the hands skill for the finest craft.

Gloves that once belonged to Rumil, lore-master of Tirion in Valinor, who first devised letters and writing among the Elves. Before even Fëanor perfected the Tengwar, Rumil created the Sarati to record the words and wisdom of the Eldar. These gloves guided his hand in that delicate work, lending precision and subtlety to the wearer's every motion.
A record keeper's gloves were made for delicate lettering and diagram work. Their enchantment lends subtlety and precision to every motion.

Brutal gauntlets forged in Angband for the orc-chieftain Gorgdaz, who led Morgoth's host against the newly-arrived Noldor. He fell in the Dagor- nuin-Giliath, the Battle under Stars, when Fëanor's fury drove the orcs back to the very gates of Angband. The gauntlets are heavy with black iron and malice, crushing anything in their grasp, and they swallow light as if hungering for the darkness of the pits where they were forged.
Brutal black iron gauntlets crush what they grip. They swallow surrounding light with the darkness of the deep furnaces where they were made.

The fur-lined gauntlets of Bregolas, Lord of Ladros in Dorthonion and elder brother of Barahir, who would father Beren One-hand. When rivers of fire poured from Thangorodrim in the Dagor Bragollach, Bregolas fought shoulder to shoulder with Angrod and Aegnor until all three fell together. His line passed to Barahir, and thence to Beren. These gauntlets ward against the bitter cold of Dorthonion's high places.
Fur lines a pair of gauntlets issued to the exposed upland watch. Their wards protect the hands against bitter cold.

Gauntlets wrought of mithril by the jewel-smiths of Gondolin, who alone in Beleriand worked that precious metal brought from Valinor. Mithril was harder than steel yet could be beaten thin as silk, and these gauntlets are proof of that art. They protect the hands while granting them the deftness needed for the finest jewel-craft, as if the wearer's fingers were made of living silver.
Fine lumesilver plates guard the hands without sacrificing delicacy. They support the deft movements needed for intricate jewel work.

The iron gauntlets of Caranthir the Dark, Lord of Thargelion, whose fiery temper was feared even among his own brothers. He grew rich from trade with the Dwarves of the Blue Mountains, yet his hands were made for war more than counting treasure. These gauntlets are crude but fearsome, and they burn with the heat of their master's unquenchable wrath.
Crude iron gauntlets were made for a commander whose temper was as dangerous as the battlefield. Heat burns within their metal.

A jewel once woven into the silver embroideries of Miriel Therinde, first wife of Finwë and mother of Fëanor. Serinde, the Broideress, she was called, for none could match her skill with needle and thread. So greatly did she spend herself in bearing Fëanor that her spirit departed to Mandos, never to return. This gem still holds the warmth of her hands and the light of the Trees under which she laboured.
A bright jewel was once sewn into a master embroiderer's ceremonial work. It retains a gentle warmth and the clear light of the old settlement workshops.

A lamp wrought by Fëanor himself for his father Finwë, High King of the Noldor. Set with crystals that captured the mingled light of Laurelin and Telperion, it was among the treasures kept at Formenos during Fëanor's exile. When Morgoth came with Ungoliant, Finwë fell defending his son's hoard, but this lamp escaped the Unlight. Its radiance pierces shadow and frees the bearer from ensnaring bonds, and its holy light unravels even the darkest curses laid upon the works of the Enemy.
Crystals within a carefully worked lamp release a radiance that pierces shadow. It frees the bearer from binding and can unravel even deeply rooted curses.

The Iron Crown of Morgoth Bauglir, forged in Angband to bear the three Silmarils, the stolen light of the Two Trees. Now all three jewels are gone, and the crown sits cold and empty—three dark sockets where stars once blazed, a monument to a glory stolen and a glory lost. Much of the Dark Lord's will was poured into its making.
The regent's immense iron crown has three empty dawnseed sockets. Cold metal remains where the weather engine's stolen power cells once burned.

The Iron Crown of Morgoth Bauglir, wrought in Angband to hold the stolen light of the world. Two sockets are empty and dark, but in the third burns still a Silmaril—a jewel of Fëanor, containing the imperishable light of the Two Trees of Valinor. It is the greatest treasure remaining in Middle-earth, and the Oath of Fëanor binds his sons to claim it.
One dawnseed still burns in the regent's iron crown, beside two empty sockets. The remaining power cell is a priceless remnant of the failed weather engine.

The Iron Crown of Morgoth Bauglir, wrought in Angband to hold the stolen light of the world. One socket gapes empty and dark, but in the other two burn still two Silmarils—jewels of Fëanor, containing the imperishable light of the Two Trees. They are the greatest treasures remaining in Middle-earth, and war and ruin have followed in their wake.
Two dawnseeds burn in the regent's iron crown, with one dark socket between them. Their radiance comes from the weather engine's surviving power cells.

The Iron Crown of Morgoth Bauglir, in which burn the three Silmarils - jewels of Fëanor, stolen from Formenos and set here by the Dark Lord himself. In them burns the imperishable light of the Two Trees of Valinor, and the Oath of Fëanor compels his sons to claim them, even unto the ruin of the world. To cut a Silmaril from the crown, stand over it and use it (u), or press (k).
Three dawnseeds blaze in the regent's iron crown, diverted from the weather engine that once served the tide settlements. To cut out a dawnseed, stand over the crown and use it (u), or press (k).

The Hammer of the Underworld, forged by Morgoth himself in the depths of Angband and wielded in his duel against Fingolfin before the gates of his fortress. Thrice it smote the earth like thunder, making great pits into which the High King stumbled, and at last Morgoth set his foot upon Fingolfin's neck and broke him. It is blackened by dark sorceries, and its wielder commands the fear of all Morgoth's servants.
A massive black hammer was forged in the deepest engine works for the regent's personal use. Its overwhelming strokes batter the ground, and its wielder commands fear among the regent's servants.
